en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Two Thousand Five Hundred Lines, entitled *Suvikrāntavikrāmiparipṛcchā*.
START SVP 1 1 The Chapter on the Introduction.
Thus have I heard.

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, together with a great saṅgha of twelve hundred and fifty monks, and with immeasurable, incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered from various buddha-fields and were bound to only one more birth.
At that time, the Blessed One, surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands, was teaching the Dharma.
Then, indeed, in that very assembly, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Suvikrāntavikrāmin was present and seated.

Rising from his seat, draping his upper robe over one shoulder, and placing his right knee upon the ground, he bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "I would ask the Blessed One a question."
“[I wish to ask] the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain point, provided that the Blessed One would grant the opportunity and allow me to have my question answered.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: “Ask, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Whatever you may desire, I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every one of those questions.
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, it is said, 'perfection of wisdom, perfection of wisdom.
To what extent, Blessed One, is it called the 'perfection of wisdom' for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas?
How, Blessed One, does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom?"
"Blessed One, how does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reach fulfillment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom?
Blessed One, how is it that when a bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom, Māra the Evil One finds no opportunity, and he understands all the works of Māra?"
“Blessed One, by dwelling in what kinds of dwellings in the perfection of wisdom does a bodhisattva mahāsattva swiftly attain the fulfillment of the qualities of omniscience?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: “Excellent, excellent, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that you ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, about the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the bodhisattvas.”
It is for the sake of the great beings (mahāsattvas),

in that you have indeed set out for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of beings— both gods and humans—
and because you desire to provide illumination for the bodhisattvas, the great beings, of the present and the future.
Then the Blessed One, although he already knew, questioned the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "Suvikrāntavikrāmin, seeing what purpose do you ask the Tathāgata this question?

When thus addressed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, for the sake of all sentient beings, for the welfare of all sentient beings, and out of compassion for all sentient beings, we ask the Tathāgata about this matter."
For what reason?
Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the grasper of all dharmas—namely, the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and perfectly enlightened buddhas.
Therefore, Blessed One, please explain the domain of the Tathāgata and the gnosis of the Tathāgata.
In that regard, those beings who are destined for the Śrāvaka vehicle will quickly realize the untainted stage;
those who are destined for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, [will likewise do so].
They will swiftly depart by means of the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas;
those who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And those who have not yet entered the fixed course of rightness and are unsettled in the three stages,

having heard this, will generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, O Blessed One, by the Tathāgata’s answering of this question regarding the perfection of wisdom, the roots of virtue of all sentient beings will be brought to birth.
Moreover, Blessed One, we do not question the Tathāgata for the sake of beings who have inferior inclinations,
nor for those with impoverished minds,
nor for those endowed with impoverished mentalities.
Not for those who are indolent,
nor for those overcome by sloth,
nor for those sunk in the mire of false views.
Not for those bound by the snares of Māra, nor for those lacking a sense of shame, nor for those who do not possess austerity.
Not for those with lost mindfulness,
not for those with deranged minds,
nor for those submerged in the mire of sensual desire.
Not for the deceitful, not for the fraudulent,
and not for those who are ungrateful.
Not for those with evil desires,
not for those of evil conduct,
nor for those who have failed in moral discipline.
Not for those of impure conduct,
nor for those with perverted views,
nor for those who wander within the domain of Māra.
Not for those who exalt themselves,
nor for those who disparage others, nor for those who value gain and honor.
not for those who are attached to bowls and robes,
nor for the deceitful, nor for the talkative;
Not those who practice divination,
nor those who use intimidation, nor those who seek to gain profit through profit.
“Blessed One, we do not question the Tathāgata on behalf of such beings.
However, Blessed One, those beings who aspire to the knowledge of the omniscient one;
who aspire to unattached knowledge, self-existent knowledge, incomparable knowledge, and unsurpassed knowledge—”
Blessed One, for those who perceive neither self nor another,
how could they ever exalt themselves or disparage others?
We [rejoice] in those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas whose pride has been destroyed, who are like bulls with their horns broken off, and from whom the thorns of shame have been extracted.
Blessed One, for the sake of those beings whose minds are base— whose thoughts are like those of the sons of outcastes, yet whose minds are equal to earth, water, fire, wind, and space—
we question the Tathāgata on behalf of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
who do not perceive even the Dharma and do not adhere to it, much less to what is non-Dharma.

Blessed One, for their sake we question the Tathāgata regarding those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are pure in intention, free from deceit, free from guile, upright, even-minded, intent on the welfare and liberation of all beings, who encourage, inspire, and gladden others,
who bear the great burden, who have mounted the Great Vehicle, who are present for the sake of the great task, and who are possessed of great compassion.

[They are] leaders, guides, and directors who bring about the welfare and happiness of all beings; who dwell without relying on any phenomena; who have no desire for any sphere of rebirth; who are liberated from the snares of all Māras; who are zealous, energetic, and vigilant; who have attained the supreme perfection of all dharmas; and who are skilled in cutting through all doubts.
"O Blessed One, for the sake of those beings—and for the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—we question the Tathāgata regarding them:
O Blessed One, what of those beings who do not even conceive of the knowledge of awakening (*bodhijñāna*), nor adhere to it, nor remain intent upon it;
who have transcended all conceit, are established on the path, have entered the path, and are teachers of the path?"
Blessed One, for the sake of those beings, we inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

Blessed One, for the purpose, benefit, happiness, and security of all beings, we inquire of the Tathāgata; Blessed One, desiring to bring about the happiness of all beings—the unsurpassed happiness, the incomparable happiness, the happiness of Nirvāṇa, the happiness of a Buddha, and the unconditioned happiness.
Therefore, Blessed One, we question the Tathāgata for the sake of cutting through the doubts of all sentient beings.
We wish to become free from doubt, Blessed One, and we wish to teach the Dharma to all sentient beings so that they may abandon their doubts, becoming themselves free from doubt, Blessed One.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, all sentient beings desire happiness and are averse to suffering;
all sentient beings seek happiness.
And we, O Blessed One, do not perceive any other happiness for all sentient beings apart from wisdom;
nor, O Blessed One, is there any other happiness for all sentient beings apart from the Bodhisattvayāna, the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, O Blessed One, perceiving this purpose and desiring to provide happiness for sentient beings, we inquire about the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
And perceiving this matter concerning the bodhisattvas, O Blessed One, we questioned the Tathāgata regarding this very point.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "Excellent, excellent, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
It is not easy to reach the limit of your virtues, you who, out of compassion for the great mass of people, inquire about this perfection of wisdom from the Tathāgata."
Therefore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, listen well and pay close attention;
I shall speak to you.
"Excellent, Blessed One! the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this: "Suvikrāntavikrāmin, as for what you say—'Blessed One, it is called "perfection of wisdom, perfection of wisdom"—to what extent, Blessed One, is it called the perfection of wisdom for bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas?
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom cannot be expressed by means of any dharma whatsoever."
For the perfection of wisdom transcends all speech;
indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is not possible to say of the perfection of wisdom: "This is that perfection of wisdom," or "The perfection of wisdom belongs to this."
"Either by this it is the perfection of wisdom, or from this it is the perfection of wisdom; for this,
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the non-perfection of all dharmas."
Therefore it is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, even wisdom itself was neither found nor apprehended by the Tathāgata.
How, moreover, could one apprehend the perfection of wisdom?
"Wisdom," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the non-knowing of all dharmas;
it is the non-cognizing of all dharmas.
Therefore it is called "wisdom.
And what, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the non-cognition of all phenomena?
It is that these all phenomena are one way, yet they are expressed in another way.
Furthermore, all phenomena are not devoid of verbal expression;
yet that which is the non-knowing of all phenomena,
and that which is the lack of cognition regarding all phenomena, [is suchness].
It cannot be expressed in words;
rather, it is called "wisdom" (prajñā) because sentient beings do not know it.
It is called "designation" (prajñapti), and for that reason it is called "wisdom" (prajñā). Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all phenomena are non-designatable.
They are non-functioning,
indefinable, and invisible;
such is their lack of cognition.
This is called "not knowing.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this wisdom is neither ignorance, nor non-ignorance,
nor is it the knowledge of ignorance.
Then he said, "It is called wisdom.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the domain of knowledge (*jñāna*), not the domain of ignorance (*ajñāna*)."
It is neither the object of ignorance nor the object of knowledge;
for knowledge has no object.
If it were the object of ignorance, [it would follow that ignorance itself would have an object].
Ignorance would [arise];
ignorance does not arise from knowledge, nor does ignorance arise from ignorance.
Nor is knowledge ignorance, nor is ignorance knowledge;
knowledge is not said to be [produced] by means of ignorance.
Nor is it said that "knowledge is known by knowledge.
For it is said that "knowledge is [known] by non-knowledge," yet there is no such thing as non-knowledge therein that can be pointed out, saying, "This is that knowledge."
Either that knowledge belongs to him, or he possesses that knowledge;
by means of that, knowledge does not exist as knowledge.
Furthermore, that knowledge does not exist as a reality,
nor is ignorance called "knowledge.
If ignorance were called "knowledge," [it would be a contradiction].
Consequently, all foolish ordinary beings would become possessors of knowledge.
However, because neither knowledge nor ignorance is apprehended, the thorough understanding of knowledge and ignorance as they truly are is itself called "knowledge."
Furthermore, that knowledge is not as it is described.
Why is that? For knowledge cannot be expressed in words, nor is knowledge an object for anyone.
For knowledge transcends all objects,
and knowledge is not an object;
this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the exposition of knowledge.
It is without location, without spatial extension;
it is by means of that knowledge that one among the wise is reckoned as "wise.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this very non-knowing, this awakening, is indeed non-cognition.
This is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is such a realization (*abhisamaya*) and direct manifestation (*sākṣātkriyā*)— this is it.
This is called supramundane wisdom, but it is not as that which is called "supramundane wisdom" [by others].
For what reason?
If even the world itself is not apprehended, how much less so supramundane wisdom?
And what need is there to mention one who will transcend the worlds by means of supramundane wisdom?
For what reason?
Because she does not perceive a world;
therefore, she does not cause anyone to cross over.
Therefore, it is called supramundane wisdom (*lokottarā prajñā*).
"World" (*loka*), Suvikrāntavikrāmin, refers to conceptual designation (*prajñapti*); the transcendence of the world is the transcendence of all conceptual designations.
That which has transcended all conceptual designations is called "supramundane."
Furthermore, transcending the world is not transcendence; non-transcendence is what transcends the world.
For what reason?
Not even the slightest dharma exists therein that is to be transcended or by which one is to transcend;
therefore it is called "supramundane.
For in the supramundane, neither the world nor the supramundane exists.
Because it is unsurpassed and there is no further crossing beyond it, it is called "supramundane.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is called the exposition of supramundane wisdom.
But it is not as it is said, that "supramundane wisdom" [is something to be described].
For what reason?
Because that which is supramundane cannot be expressed in words; it has transcended them.
Therein, nothing further remains to be transcended;
therefore, it is called supramundane wisdom.
In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, as for that penetrative wisdom (*nirvedhikā prajñā*), what does that wisdom penetrate?
There is nothing here whatsoever to be penetrated.
If there were anything to be pierced through, it would be designated thus: "This is that wisdom which pierces through.
But nothing is pierced through, nor is anything not pierced through.
No answer whatsoever is found that could be pierced;
as for "it pierces," here there is nothing that pierces nor anything that is not pierced,
and here there is nothing that is being pierced nor anything that is not being pierced.
Therefore it is said that "it pierces through.
Herein, nothing reaches an end, nor does it reach a middle; therefore it is said that "it pierces through."
It penetrates; thus it is called "penetrating wisdom" (*nirvedhikā prajñā*). It penetrates, yet it does not run anywhere, it does not run about, nor does it run on.
Therefore it is called "penetrating.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, as for what this penetrating wisdom penetrates:
whatever there is of seeing, [it penetrates that].
He penetrates all that.
By what does he penetrate it?
He penetrates it by means of wisdom (prajñā).
How does one penetrate by means of wisdom?
One penetrates it as having the characteristic of a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*).
Whatever has the characteristic of a conceptual designation—
"All that is without characteristics; 'without characteristics' means having the characteristic of designation.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whoever is endowed with such wisdom as this penetrates [reality].
He pierces the triple world. How does he pierce it? He pierces through [it] as the triple world being without elements (*adhātuka*).
For here no one pierces any element; he pierces it as the "elementless" within the triple world.
By means of this, the triple world is thus pierced through.
This is called being endowed with penetrative wisdom (*nairvedhikī prajñā*).
And how is one endowed with penetrative wisdom?
For there is nothing unwholesome that remains to be penetrated.
He penetrates everything as wholesome and transcends it by means of penetrative wisdom (*nairvedhikī prajñā*).
Endowed with such penetrative wisdom, whatever he sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, or cognizes, [he regards it all as wholesome].
One penetrates all of that.
How does one penetrate it? As impermanent, as suffering, as a boil, as a disease, as a thorn, as empty, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, and as subject to destruction.
Because it is subject to disintegration, moving, fragile, non-self, unarisen, unceasing, and without characteristics— this, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is called "become cooled" and "without the arrow.
Just as, for example, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is a kind of medicine named "the Arrow-Remover," so it is with this.
Just as that [arrow] from which it is fixed draws out and pierces through all other shafts,

even so a monk endowed with such qualities is free from arrows, has become cooled, is possessed of penetrative wisdom (*nairvedhikī prajñā*), dwells in the utter transcendence of *saṃsāra*, possesses penetrative wisdom, is dispassionate, and has transcended all the snares of Māra.
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, wherever a vajra is cast for the purpose of piercing, it pierces that very thing;
even so, the mind of a monk is embraced by the wisdom of penetration through the diamond-like samādhi.
He penetrates all those things upon which he establishes [his mind] and in which he causes it to circulate.
Endowed with that penetrative wisdom— supramundane, leading to the complete destruction of suffering— he is called "one who is unstained and possesses the three types of knowledge."
"Knowledge," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a designation for the subsiding of ignorance;
"thorough comprehension of ignorance" is a designation for the cessation of the aggregate of suffering.
Just as, for example, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a physician who is learned, discerning, and wise [employs] the appropriate medical treatises...
He should be endowed with investigation, skilled in all medicines, skilled in the arising of all diseases, and a liberator from all suffering.
Whichever patient he treats, he liberates that very person.
For what reason?
For he is skilled in all medicines, skilled in the origin of all diseases, and the liberator from all illnesses.
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the third knowledge conduces to the pacification of all ignorance and conduces to the emergence from all suffering.
It leads to the pacification of all aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is called supramundane wisdom that penetrates to the ultimate.
And this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, was spoken by me with reference to the Saṅgha: "Wisdom is indeed supreme in the world, for it leads to penetration;
through it one correctly understands the exhaustion of existence and birth."
Thus it is said:
"The complete exhaustion of existence and birth"—Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for what is this a designation? It is a designation for the penetration of arising and passing away.
And what is the penetration of arising and passing away? It is the penetration of arising and passing away by realizing that whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation.
"Arising," O Suvikrāmin, is a designation for production; "passing away" is a designation for cessation;
yet arising and passing away do not occur in the manner in which they are described.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whatever is an arising is not subject to the nature of arising;
for indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no arising whatsoever of the Equal One.
Nor does it arise;
it simply conforms to equality.
Therefore, it is called "origination."
"Followed by equanimity," Suvikrāntavikrāmin— herein nothing whatsoever arises or comes into being;
that which is its intrinsic nature is not a self-originated existence.
That is cessation;
and therein there is no cessation of anything whatsoever, but rather cessation immediately following origination.
Where there is no arising, there is no cessation;
that is cessation.
Thus, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that penetration of arising and ceasing which is for the sake of non-arising and non-ceasing—
that is the penetration of ceasing.
Therefore it is called "the penetration of arising and ceasing."
"Penetration," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is this thorough knowledge of dependent origination:
whatever phenomenon arises in dependence upon something, that very phenomenon does not exist in dependence upon that very thing.
This is called the penetration of dependent origination.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this thorough comprehension of dependent origination is indicated by non-arising as it truly is;
for dependent origination is indeed non-arising.
Non-arising is sameness;
therefore it is called dependent origination.
Where there is no arising, [there is dependent origination].
In that regard, from what does cessation arise?
Non-cessation is cessation; it is the awakening to dependent origination.
That which is non-arising is called dependent origination.
That which is non-arising is non-production;
that which is non-production is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Its cessation does not exist.
That for which cessation does not exist is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
And he by whom non-arising is known no longer produces [anything], nor does he realize cessation.
He who does not produce [anything] does not cease [anything];
for it is only when there is production that cessation is known.
By means of that [realization], all phenomena are known, seen, penetrated, and realized as being precisely ceased.
Therefore, it is said that "cessation has been realized."
"O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, 'knowledge of destruction' (kṣayajñāna) means that ignorance has been destroyed;
therefore it is called 'knowledge of destruction.
By what has it been destroyed?"
It is exhausted by way of being inexhaustible;
one does not perceive its exhaustion.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the departure from ignorance.
Therefore, it is called the "knowledge of destruction.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the full comprehension of ignorance;
therefore, it is said that the destruction of ignorance is the knowledge of destruction.
For ignorance is neither destruction nor non-destruction.
This disappearance, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is what will be known;
therefore it is called "knowledge of destruction."
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are;
therefore it is called "departure.
Nothing else whatsoever is perceived therein, other than this departure from that [false] cognition.
Knowledge itself is not apprehended; how much less so ignorance? For whomsoever there is liberation, [it is from this].
Therefore it is called the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), but not in the manner in which it is [commonly] spoken of;
for one who possesses this knowledge of destruction, however, [it is as follows].
For that, there is no conventional designation whatsoever;
rather, this is merely a description, such as "the destruction of ignorance" or "the knowledge of destruction.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, he who has realized this investigation into the inexhaustible knowledge of destruction regarding all phenomena is one who is free from the knowledge of destruction.
He has attained the inexhaustible limit;
the limitless is the limit of nirvāṇa, and not as it is otherwise described.
Nirvāṇa is ineffable and the cessation of all conventional discourse.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the teaching on the realm of nirvāṇa;
it is not, however, as it has been described.
For the realm of nirvāṇa is indeed ineffable; it transcends all description, and the realm of nirvāṇa is utterly cut off from all description.
This is called the description of supramundane, penetrative wisdom—that which is this realm of nirvāṇa.
And yet, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the realm of nirvāṇa is neither located in a place nor situated in a specific region;
this is its explanation.
In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, what is the perfection of wisdom?
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither a near shore nor a far shore to the perfection of wisdom.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if either this shore or the further shore of the perfection of wisdom were to be apprehended,

the Tathāgata would have pointed out either this shore or the further shore of wisdom. But, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, neither this shore of the perfection of wisdom is apprehended, nor is its further shore apprehended.
Therefore, its further shore is not pointed out.
However, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, "perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitā) refers to the perfection of all dharmas and of the activities of knowledge;
for that reason, it is called the perfection of wisdom.
But it is not as it is said;
for the perfection of wisdom is not present through speech or through action.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is inexpressible.
This is the awakening to all phenomena;
and that which is awakening is non-contradiction.
For what reason?
Because therein nothing at all has been awakened to, nor has anything been penetrated.
For awakening is the equality of realization and penetration; it is called "awakening" because of the realization of all phenomena.
And how is there the realization of all phenomena?
Herein there is no awakening whatsoever, nor is there any realization whatsoever.
For what reason?
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if awakening were to be apprehended,
then awakening would be found within awakening.
Moreover, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, awakening does not exist within awakening;
in this way, this awakening is to be fully realized.
Because there is no subsequent awakening and no penetration, it is called "awakening."
Furthermore, it is not as it is said that all phenomena are unawakened to and unpenetrated;
rather, by this awakening, no phenomenon exists by way of its own intrinsic nature.
This is called "awakening."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, awakening was not apprehended by the Tathāgata,
nor was awakening made known by the Tathāgata; awakening is unmanifestable and unproclaimable.
Furthermore, enlightenment was neither known nor produced by the Tathāgata;
for enlightenment is unborn and unmanifested.
Nor is enlightenment the domain of anyone.
Furthermore, in awakening there is no sentient being whatsoever, nor even the designation of a "sentient being.
Since neither a sentient being nor the designation of a "sentient being" exists therein,
how can one say, "This is a bodhisattva"?
Is this the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva?
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no awakening within awakening,
nor is there any sentient being within awakening.
For this awakening has transcended;
this awakening is unarisen;
this awakening is unconditioned.
This awakening is without characteristics; within it, no sentient being exists and none is apprehended.
Awakening is not designated by way of a sentient being;
for awakening is said to be the realization of the absence of a sentient being. By whomsoever it is known that awakening is the absence of a sentient being—
He is called a "bodhisattva.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva is not characterized by the perception of a sentient being.
Because he has eliminated the perception of a "being," he is called a bodhisattva,
yet not in the manner in which he is described.
For what reason?
For a bodhisattva is indeed ineffable;
for a bodhisattva is devoid of the intrinsic nature of a sentient being; for awakening is devoid of the notion of a sentient being.
One by whom awakening is thus known is called a bodhisattva. How is awakening known?
This awakening has transcended;
this awakening is not something to be produced; for this awakening is indeed without arising and without cessation.
Awakening does not make itself known by awakening, nor is awakening something to be made known.
Awakening is called that which cannot be made known, cannot be designated, and cannot be brought into being.
Because they have understood and awakened through non-conceptualization for the sake of severing conceptual construction,
they are called "bodhisattvas," but not in the manner in which the term is otherwise commonly used.
Why is that? Because of the absence of a sentient being (*niḥsattvatvāt*).
If a bodhisattva were to be apprehended, then awakening would be something apprehended—this would be that awakening.
Thinking, "These are beings," yet because of the realization and awakening to the absence of being, the lack of a self-nature of beings, and the non-existence of beings, one is called a Bodhisattva.
Because of the state of being without a self-nature, through the cultivation of the perception of beings and the cultivation of the perception of non-beings, one is called a Bodhisattva.
Why is that?
"The realm of sentient beings" is a designation for the non-existence of sentient beings;
for indeed, no sentient being is found within a sentient being.
Because the realm of sentient beings does not exist as a real entity; for if there were a sentient being within the realm of sentient beings,
it would not be called the "realm of sentient beings."
This "realm of sentient beings" is a designation for that which is not a realm;
for the realm of sentient beings is indeed without a realm.
If there were a realm of sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings, [it would be a contradiction].
That body would be possessed of a living being; or else,
if it were an element released from the realm of sentient beings, then the realm of sentient beings would indeed be without elements.
The realm (dhātu) becomes a conventional term through linguistic convention; for a realm does not exist within the realm of sentient beings,
nor does the realm of sentient beings exist apart from the realm of sentient beings.
For all phenomena are without constituent elements (adhātuka).
It was with this in mind that I spoke: "Neither a decrease nor an increase in the realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu) is perceived.
For what reason?
Because the realm of sentient beings is non-existent, because the realm of sentient beings is secluded;
and just as no decrease or increase of the realm of sentient beings is perceived, so it is here.
In this way, neither deficiency nor fullness is perceived even among all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). For there is no ultimate establishment (*pariniṣpatti*) of any phenomena whatsoever,
by which they could possess either deficiency or fullness.
This very realization of all phenomena is called the "realization of all phenomena.
And it was with this in mind that I spoke these words: that neither decrease nor increase of the realm of sentient beings is perceived.
In this way, neither deficiency nor fullness is perceived even among all phenomena;
and that which is the non-deficiency and non-fullness of all phenomena is due to their lack of ultimate establishment.
That itself is the non-deficiency and non-fullness of the Buddha-dharmas as well.
Thus, because of the realization of all dharmas, there is the non-deficiency and non-fullness of the Buddha-dharmas;
because all dharmas are neither deficient nor full, they are called "Buddha-dharmas."
Therefore, that is a designation for the qualities of a Buddha;
for indeed, the qualities of a Buddha cannot be made deficient or complete by anyone.
Why is that?
This is the awakening to all phenomena;
and in that awakening to all phenomena, there is neither deficiency nor fullness of any phenomenon whatsoever.
"All phenomena" is a designation for the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
yet there is neither deficiency nor fullness in the realm of phenomena.
For what reason?
For the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is infinite.
Indeed, no difference is perceived between the realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu) and the realm of phenomena;
nor is any deficiency or fullness perceived or found in either the realm of sentient beings or the realm of phenomena.
This very realization is called "awakening.
Therefore it is said: "Neither deficiency nor fullness is perceived in the qualities of a Buddha."
“Non-deficiency and non-excess,” Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a designation for seeing things as they truly are, which is free from conceptual construction.
In that regard, it is impossible for anyone to either subtract or add anything.
Such is this realization.
This is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).
"Awakening," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a characteristic of a Buddha.
In what way is it a characteristic of a Buddha?
The absence of characteristics in the characteristics of all phenomena— this is the characteristic of a Buddha;
for awakening is indeed without characteristics, being free from the intrinsic nature of characteristics.
That which is such an awakening is called "awakening," but not in the manner as it is [conventionally] spoken of.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is because of the awakening to these very dharmas that one is called a "bodhisattva.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whoever, not knowing and not understanding these dharmas, claims for himself the title of "bodhisattva," for such a person the stage of a bodhisattva is far removed.
The qualities of a bodhisattva are far removed;
such a person deceives the world with its gods, humans, and asuras by means of the name "bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if a bodhisattva were to exist by mere words alone, [he would be a fraud].
By that [logic], all sentient beings would also be bodhisattvas.
However, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is not a mere matter of words to say "this is the bodhisattva stage.
Nor is it possible to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through speech alone.
For awakening is not attained through vocal action,
nor are the qualities of a bodhisattva;
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all sentient beings course toward awakening.
They neither know nor understand;
therefore, they are not called bodhisattvas. For what reason?
For sentient beings do not realize that they are non-existent;
if they were to know this, they would become bodhisattvas through their own conduct.
Furthermore, beings who are inverted do not understand their own conduct, their own domain, or their own sphere of experience.
If they were to understand their own conduct,
they would no longer engage in any conceptual construction whatsoever.
By means of those practices of conceptualization, all foolish ordinary beings course in non-existent objects;
they even take awakening as an object and conceive of it as such.
For those who course in objects and course in conceptualization, whence can there be awakening?
Whence come the dharmas of a bodhisattva?
Those who understand the Dharma in this way no longer course in unreal objective referents.
They no longer conceive of any dharma whatsoever;
therefore it is said that "non-practice is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Bodhisattvas do not course in conceptualization nor in discursive differentiation.
Where there is neither conceptualization nor discursive thought, there is no practice whatsoever;
and where there is non-conceptualization, [there is no practice].
In that state, there is no practice for anyone;
for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all practice is non-conceptual practice.
All forms of conceit are without objective support.
Knowing all phenomena in this way, he no longer courses or ranges within objective referents or conceptual constructions.
This is the practice of bodhisattvas by way of non-practice.
For it is thus, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that they understand and awaken to phenomena.
Therefore, they are called "bodhisattvas."
"Non-being" (asattva) is a designation for a bodhisattva, for by him all perceptions of beings have been thoroughly cultivated away. Why is that?

For by him all sentient beings have been known as non-existent, all sentient beings as devoid of the nature of sentient beings, all sentient beings as sentient beings through inversion, and all sentient beings as merely imagined sentient beings.
All sentient beings have non-existent objects of perception; all sentient beings have lost their own proper conduct;
all sentient beings consist of ignorance and formative forces.
For what reason?
Because they construct those very dharmas which do not exist for all sentient beings.
Therefore it is said that all sentient beings are beings of ignorance and formative forces (*avidyā-saṃskāra*).
What phenomenon does not exist?
Neither "I," nor "mine," nor "I am"—no such phenomenon exists at all.
If there were any dharma— whether "I," or "mine," or "I am"— then by that, beings would have come into existence.
But since, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no such dharma whatsoever, [beings do not exist].
He who thinks "I" or "mine" or "I am"—
by him it is said that all sentient beings are non-existent;
for all sentient beings are merely sentient beings conditioned by ignorance.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there exists no such thing as a phenomenon called a "sentient being" for whom there could be the thought "I," or "mine," or "I am.
And because it does not exist, therefore sentient beings are said to be non-existent.
"Unreal" is a designation for non-existent beings;
or rather, because they are attached to the unreal notion of a "being," it is therefore said that "beings are unreal."
"Unreal," Suvikrāntavikrāmin—herein there is nothing that has become real, nor anything produced.
For all dharmas are unreal and unproduced.
It is therein that unreal beings, through their attachment, become bound.
Therefore, they are called "beings with unreal objects.
Because they do not understand that very conduct of their own, they are called "unreal beings.
Furthermore, because of the awakening to that which was previously unawakened, they are called "bodhisattvas."
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, he who thus understands these phenomena is called a bodhisattva.
"Bodhisattva" is a designation for one who has awakened after [the Buddhas].
By whom all dharmas are known as Buddhas.
How are they known?
As non-existent.
They are unarisen and non-erroneous;
they are not as they are imagined by foolish ordinary people,
nor are they as they are apprehended by foolish ordinary people.
Therefore they are called "bodhisattvas. For what reason?
Because awakening is indeed neither conceptualized nor discriminated.
For awakening is unconstructed; for awakening is non-apprehensible.
Indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, awakening was not attained by the Tathāgata.
Because of the non-apprehension of all phenomena and because of the non-perception of all phenomena, it is called "awakening" (bodhi).
Thus it is called the awakening of a Buddha, but not in the manner in which it is described.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those who generate the thought for awakening thinking, "We shall generate this thought for the sake of awakening," and who conceive of awakening as something [external],
thinking, "There exists that awakening for which we shall generate the thought"—
they are not called bodhisattvas.
They are called "beings who have arisen.
For what reason?
Because, being attached to arising and attached to the mind, they become attached to awakening.
Those who generate the mind set on awakening, yet remain attached to that thought of awakening, are called "bodhisattvas who are fixated on the thought of awakening.
This is because they engage in volitional construction.
Therefore, they generate the mind for awakening;
for that reason, they are called "beings of volitional formation."
They are not bodhisattvas. For what reason?
They are said to be "beings who have arisen."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is not possible to generate the mind for awakening;
for awakening is unarisen,
and awakening is without mind.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, they adhere only to arising;
they do not understand non-arising.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the sameness of arising is reality itself.
That which is the evenness of mind and that which is the evenness of reality,
and that which is the evenness of reality and that which is evenness— that is awakening.
And wherein there is suchness, [that is awakening].
In that regard, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever.
Yet, having conceptually constructed the mind and being attached to awakening, they generate the thought of awakening dualistically.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the mind is not one thing and awakening another.
Enlightenment is not in the mind, nor is the mind in enlightenment; that which is enlightenment and that which is the mind— [are one].
That is suchness and suchness-ness;
herein there is neither awakening nor mind,
nor is awakening apprehended.
There is neither arising nor non-arising;
for that reason, he is called a "bodhisattva" and is called a "being as it truly is."
He is called a "Great Being.
For what reason? Because that which is unreal—
She was understood by him.
And what is that unreality? For this entire world is indeed unreal.
Alas, this worldly arrangement is comprised of the unreal, it is unreal, and it has not come into being. Why is there the arising of the unreal?
There is no arising whatsoever of that which is unreal.
For that which has not come into being is unreal;
therefore it is said that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and are unreal.
He by whom this is thus known—
He is called a "being as it truly is" (yathābhūtasattva). He does not adhere to reality within reality;
therefore, he is called a "being as it truly is."
But it is not as it is said.
For what reason?
Because in reality, there is no such thing as a sentient being or a great being (mahāsattva).
For whoever plunges into the Mahāyāna is called a *mahāsattva*.
And what is the Mahāyāna?
All knowledge is the Mahāyāna.
And what is all knowledge?
Whatever conditioned knowledge there is, whether mundane knowledge or supramundane knowledge,
by means of that he is called a "Mahāsattva."
For what reason?
Because his great perception of a sentient being has vanished;
therefore, he is called a "Great Being" (mahāsattva).
The great aggregate of ignorance has vanished for him;
therefore he is called a "Great Being.
The great aggregate of formative forces has vanished for him.
Therefore he is called a "Great Being" (mahāsattva);
the great mass of ignorance has departed from him,
therefore he is called a "Great Being."
The great mass of suffering of the Great Being has vanished;
therefore, he is called a "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*).
For those, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, who have reviled the notion of a "Great Being," [they too shall attain this state].
They do not perceive the mind, nor do they perceive mental factors;
they understand the nature of the mind,
yet they do not perceive awakening.
They do not discern the factors conducive to awakening nor the intrinsic nature of awakening;
with an unknowing mind, they do not perceive awakening.
They do not perceive the mind apart from awakening, nor do they perceive the mind in awakening,
nor do they perceive awakening in the mind.
Those who analyze in this way do not cultivate anything, nor do they deconstruct; they do not perceive even phenomena, they do not conceive of them, and they do not adhere to them.
For they indeed generate the mind for awakening;
and those, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, who thus generate the mind for awakening, are called "bodhisattvas."
And they do not turn back from awakening.
For what reason?
Because they are established in awakening itself.
That which is thus neither of awakening, nor of the mind, nor of its arising—
They do not perceive any differentiation within cessation;
for herein no one perceives anything,
and no one becomes attached to anything.
No one falls into conceptual construction;
those who, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, thus give rise to a mind of resolute faith and liberation, they are called true bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those who, perceiving what is called "mind" and perceiving what is called "enlightenment," generate the thought of enlightenment,
are far from enlightenment.
They are not near to awakening.
But those, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, who perceive that awakening is neither far nor near, they are near to awakening.
And by them the thought of awakening has been generated.
It was with reference to this that I spoke: "For whoever understands the non-dual self, he understands the Buddha and the Dharma."
For what reason?
Because he cultivates the self-nature of all phenomena,
by which, through the thorough knowledge of non-duality, all phenomena are thoroughly known.
For all phenomena are fixed by their own nature as self;
whoever understands the non-dual dharma understands the qualities of a Buddha.
Through the thorough knowledge of non-dual phenomena comes the thorough knowledge of the Buddha-qualities;
through the thorough knowledge of the self comes the thorough knowledge of the entire triple world.
"Thorough knowledge of the self," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the perfection of all phenomena.
And what is the further shore of all phenomena?
It is that which does not perceive a near shore, does not conceive of a further shore, and does not adhere to a further shore;
through the thorough knowledge of this, one is said to have "gone to the further shore."
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this bodhisattva stage is to be understood not as it is described;
that is the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom.
In this, there is not even the slightest thing to be gone toward or to be realized;
for herein neither coming nor going is perceived. Thus it is said.
The First Chapter: The Introduction, from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom.

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those who are conceited and who dwell upon signs will be terrified by this teaching.

Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, there is no access here for those who are conceited; it is not their domain. They will not, however, be terrified by this."
For what reason?
Those who have fallen into the hands of evil friends are terrified;
they have no access here, for this is not their domain.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, those who have set out for the abandonment of overweening pride and are striving for the abandonment of overweening pride will indeed be terrified here.
For what reason?
Through wisdom that transcends conceit, they seek the state of being free from conceit and they seek the abandonment of conceit.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, those who do not perceive conceit, do not observe it, do not think about it, and do not adhere to it, will not be terrified by anything.
Nor will they experience any terror anywhere.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, this teaching of the Dharma was not set forth for the sake of those who are conceited;
for there is no room here, Venerable Ānanda, for those who are conceited.
And those who are striving and exerting themselves for the abandonment of conceit—
“conceit,” venerable Ānanda, is a designation for the superimposition of a special status. Those who course in conceit, [do not understand this].
They practice by superimposing authority;
they are not practitioners of equanimity.
Even those who practice with equanimity have doubt regarding this Dharma.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, those who perceive neither the even nor the uneven,
who do not conceive of either the even or the uneven,
and who likewise do not adhere to either the even or the uneven— [they do not perceive the world as eternal].
They will not be terrified anywhere, they will not be frightened, nor will they fall into a state of terror.
"Venerable Ānanda, this is inaccessible to all foolish ordinary people; it is not their domain.
Venerable Ānanda, in this matter, all foolish ordinary people do not find even a way of entry. Furthermore, Ānanda, this is inaccessible even to those belonging to the vehicle of the disciples."
And those who belong to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and course in profound dharmas—
for them also there is no access here.

Furthermore, O Venerable Ānanda, those who belong to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas but course in signs, being unattended by spiritual friends and fallen into the hands of evil friends— [for them also there is no access here].
Even for them, these stainless dharmas are inaccessible and beyond their sphere.
However, Venerable Ānanda, this excludes those followers of the Śrāvaka-vehicle (or the Bodhisattva-vehicle) who have seen the truth,
who are supported by spiritual friends, and who have faith in the profound Dharma.
Those who practice in accordance with these dharmas,
those who penetrate and enter into these dharmas;
furthermore, O Venerable Ānanda, those bodhisattvas who are free from signs, who course in the signless, who course in non-differentiation, and who have utterly emerged into profound dharmas—
Those who do not perceive a mind in this way, nor awakening, do not create a differentiation of any dharma,
nor do they observe it.
Regarding such dharmas as these, they have neither sluggishness nor doubt.
For what reason?
Because they abide in conformity with all dharmas, not in opposition to them.
From whatever points they are questioned regarding the dharmas, from those very points they will respond in accordance with the truth and provide a coherent synthesis in accordance with the truth.
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Ānanda: "It is even so, Ānanda, just as this Śāradvatīputra has explained.
Ānanda, those who are conceited have no ground for this teaching of the Dharma."

For it is not within the scope of one to enter this awakening of a Buddha; Ānanda, this awakening of a Buddha is conformable [to the truth]. Indeed, Ānanda, the minds of beings with inferior inclinations do not turn toward sublime dharmas, that is, the dharmas of a Buddha.
For those, Ānanda, who have inferior inclinations, who are conceited, and who stand in opposition to the enlightenment of a Buddha—
they proceed under the influence of their conceit.

Ānanda, this assembly is pure; they have performed services for previous Victors, planted roots of merit, attended upon many Buddhas, are devoted to the profound Dharma, and practice the profound Dharma. For the Tathāgata has full confidence in this assembly and teaches the Dharma boldly;
he teaches the Dharma without having anything to conceal.
"Ānanda, this assembly is refined, free from gravel, grit, and pebbles; it has attended upon many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and is established in the essence.
'Grit and pebbles,' Ānanda, is a designation for foolish ordinary people, for whom there is no room within these teachings."
"Parpaṭa," Ānanda, is a designation for persons who are conceited. This assembly, Ānanda, is free from conceit and has emerged through great roots of merit.
Ānanda, it is just as when the nāga king Anavatapta becomes joyful and filled with gladness and happiness; at that time,
he enjoys himself in his own abode with the five strands of sensual pleasure, and being greatly delighted in his own abode, he releases a great rain of water endowed with the eight qualities.

At that time, even those who are his sons, being joyful in their respective mansions and endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, while playing, let loose a great rain; in the very same way, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, lets loose the great rain of Dharma, these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are his eldest sons.

They too, having gone from this world-system to their respective buddha-fields, release a great rain of Dharma and pour down a great shower of Dharma before those Tathāgatas, beginning with this collection of Dharma.
Ānanda, it is just as when the nāga king Sāgara becomes joyful.
Then, in his own abode, he releases great torrents of rain;
and those nāgas who are the permanent residents in that abode receive those showers of rain.
They become contented,
and by means of those showers of rain, they experience happiness;
even those who are his sons [experience it].
They endure those showers of rain and,
through those showers of rain, they obtain joy.
For what reason is that?
For those showers of rain, Ānanda, are indeed unbearable for other nāgas;
nor would other nāgas experience comfort from those showers of rain, nor would they be satisfied by them.
In the same way, Ānanda, those who dwell in the jewel of the Dharma of the Tathāgata,
and those who are the eldest sons of the Tathāgata— the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have cultivated roots of merit, possess noble intentions, and have emerged from the profound method of the Dharma—
they are able to withstand this great rain of the method of the Dharma from the Tathāgata.

Having heard this, they become elated, joyful, and thrilled, and experience happiness. Ānanda, it is for this purpose that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, utters the great lion’s roar in this pure assembly and pours down the great rain of Dharma.
It is just as if, Ānanda, a universal monarch possessed a vast accumulation of many treasuries of jewels,
and he had many sons who were noble by birth and pure of lineage;
having brought them all together, he would divide and bestow that store of jewels equally upon them.
And he would not deceive any of his sons.
Indeed, being thus shared out, they would generate even greater affection and confidence toward that universal monarch,
and they would perceive themselves as sharing the same purpose as the universal monarch.

In the same way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata also— the King of Dharma, the Lord of Dharma, the Self-Existent— having assembled these sons, distributes this treasury of the jewel of the Dharma among them and does not deceive anyone; they, in turn, produce toward me an even greater measure of love, faith, and reverence.
And through their consistency in purpose, they remain so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted.

Ānanda, it is not possible for other beings— those of inferior inclinations, those who are conceited, those whose conduct is based on views, those whose conduct is based on signs, those whose conduct is based on the view of apprehension, those struck by the pride of "I am," those overwhelmed by passion, hatred, and delusion, and those who have set out upon a wrong path— to [grasp] this jewel of the Dharma. Indeed, Ānanda, the wealth of a universal monarch does not please beings of inferior inclinations.

Ānanda, only those who are sons of a universal monarch find pleasure in the wealth of a universal monarch. Ānanda, what would poor beings do with the jewel of the wheel, or the jewel of the elephant, or the jewel of the horse, or the jewel of the gem, or the jewel of the woman, or the jewel of the householder, or the jewel of the counselor?

Or they may have need of noble garments, or noble gold, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, corals, native gold, and silver; yet even having obtained these, they are so delighted that they are unable to enjoy them.
Or they sell it at a low price, and through lack of skill, they even discard it.
Why is that? Because they are not experts in jewels.
Moreover, Ānanda, poor beings do not even recognize jewels, [thinking], "This jewel has this name.

In the very same way, Ānanda, those who are the sons of the Tathāgata— the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas who have seen the truths— they are indeed the recipients of this treasury of the jewel of the Dharma.

If they find pleasure in and accept this jewel of the Dharma— which is connected with non-apprehension and emptiness, and connected with the qualities of a Buddha— then they alone perform the work by means of it. Ānanda, what will those poor beings— who are devoid of learning, who have erred regarding learning, who are foolish, and who lack vision— do with this treasury of the jewel of the Dharma?
Having obtained it, they will discard it, or they will think it should be given to others;
for indeed, Ānanda, whether they be Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, bamboo-workers, or any other beings living in poverty, having obtained a noble jewel, they do not consume it themselves.
They either sell them for a high price or discard them.
"Poor beings," Ānanda, is a designation for all the founders of other sects,
as well as for those disciples of other sects.

"O Ānanda, 'poor beings' is a designation for all foolish commoners who are submerged in the mire of views, who are characterized by apprehension, who are attached to bondage, who conduct themselves according to signs, and who have set out upon a wrong path; indeed, O Ānanda, those who, having obtained this jewel of the Dharma, are unable to enjoy it or even cast it aside."
Or they give it away to others in vain.
But those, Ānanda, who obtain the jewel of the Dharma— sons of the Buddha, who move within the sphere of the Buddha, and who abide in the non-interruption of the lineage of the Tathāgata—
they indeed [possess] this...
They enjoy the jewel of the Dharma;
having obtained it, they do not let it perish,
and they maintain the perception of it as a jewel.
For indeed, Ānanda, a jackal does not enjoy the lion’s roar;
but those, Ānanda, who are lion cubs produced by a great lion, they enjoy that great lion’s roar.
In the same way, Ānanda, all foolish ordinary people with false views are like jackals;
they are not capable of digesting the great lion’s roar of the Tathāgata, the Dharma of the Great Lion, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those who are the cubs of the Perfectly Awakened One, produced by the Great Buddha-Siṃha while he himself was eating,
they enjoy this Great Lion’s Roar of the Perfectly Awakened One, and they shall continue to enjoy it.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: “It is marvelous, Blessed One, how exceedingly pure this assembly of the Tathāgata has gathered!
It is most marvelous, Blessed One, that this assembly of the Tathāgata is so utterly pure.”

“O Blessed One, this assembly is an assembly that cannot be crushed by the assembly of the Self-Existent One; it is an assembly like a diamond; it is an assembly that is immovable, unshakable, and imperturbable.

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāradvatīputra: “Śāradvatīputra, you are proclaiming the virtues of this assembly. He replied: “Indeed, O Blessed One, it is not possible for me to proclaim the virtues of this assembly.”
"For what reason? Blessed One, this assembly is like Mount Sumeru, endowed with infinite qualities.
The Blessed One said, "Just so, Śāradvatīputra, this assembly is endowed with infinite qualities."
For even by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, it is not possible to fully grasp the limit of the virtues of this assembly,
let alone by other beings.
Śāradvatīputra, this assembly was not convened by the Tathāgata [for his own sake].
Nor did the Tathāgata have any exertion or effort regarding this assembly;
rather, by their own roots of merit, having heard my name, this assembly has gathered here.
No one in this assembly was dispatched or requested by the Tathāgata.
Impelled by their own roots of virtue, they have come to this assembly;
such is the nature of things.
Indeed, at a Dharma teaching of this kind, there must necessarily be a gathering of great beings such as these.
Śāradvatīputra, whatever other Buddhas, Blessed Ones, shall proclaim this Bodhisattvapiṭaka that cuts through all doubts,
they too will have such an assembly; indeed,
an assembly circle of exactly this kind must necessarily be cultivated for this teaching of the Dharma.
This is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The second chapter, titled "Ānanda," in the Noble Perfection of Wisdom.
