Then the Blessed One addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "Suvikrāntavikrāmin, regarding 'perfection of wisdom, perfection of wisdom,' what is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva?
It is that perfection which belongs to all dharmas."
It cannot be fully described;
however, I shall describe it in such a way that you will come to understand it.
Just as conventional expressions will appear in the Prajñāpāramitā:
"Form is not the Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth.
In the same way, there is no feeling, no perception, and no mental formations.
Consciousness is not the perfection of wisdom,
nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in form, up to and including: nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in consciousness.
For what reason? Because,
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the limit of form is not form.
And so on; likewise, that which is the further shore of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
That is not consciousness;
as is the limit of form, so is form.
Just as there is a further shore for feeling, perception, and mental formations, so too is there a further shore for consciousness.
And as is the limit of consciousness,
so is the limit of all phenomena;
and that which is the limit of all phenomena—
Those are not all dharmas;
and as is the limit of all dharmas,
so are all dharmas.
In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the statement “that which is the limit of form is not form” is taught as the dissociation from form;
the statement “as is the limit of form, so is form” is taught as the teaching on the intrinsic nature of form;
thus has it been taught according to the reality of form.
This has been taught as the intrinsic nature of form;
this has been taught as the non-apprehension of form.
The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
“That which is the further shore of consciousness is not that consciousness”—this indeed indicates the dissociation from consciousness.
“As is the further shore of consciousness, so is consciousness”—this indicates the instruction on the intrinsic nature of consciousness;
it indicates the suchness of consciousness, the primordial nature of consciousness, and the non-apprehension of consciousness.
“That which is the further shore of all phenomena is not those all phenomena”—this has been taught as the dissociation from all phenomena.
“As is the further shore of all phenomena, so are all phenomena”—this has been taught as the teaching on the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
this has been taught as the suchness of all phenomena, the primordial nature of all phenomena, and the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
And just as the suchness of all phenomena, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and the non-apprehension of all phenomena are [identical],
so too is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom does not rely on form,
nor does it rely on feeling, nor does it rely on perception.
It does not depend on formative forces,
nor does it depend on consciousness;
nor is the perfection of wisdom situated at a distance from form, whether internally, externally, or in between the two.
It does not abide internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, as something remote from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is neither conjoined with form,
nor is it disjoined from form;
it is neither conjoined with feeling, nor conjoined with mental formations.
The perfection of wisdom is not conjoined with consciousness,
nor is the perfection of wisdom disjoined from consciousness.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from any dharma whatsoever.
Furthermore, that which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of form— its non-falsity, its non-otherness, its suchness as it truly is—
this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Likewise, that which is the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— its non-falsity, its non-otherness, its suchness as it truly is— [is the perfection of wisdom].
That is the perfection of wisdom.
"Form," O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is that which is devoid of form. For what reason?
For form does not exist within form;
and that which is non-existence is this very perfection of wisdom.
In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness— O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, these are devoid of consciousness.
For what reason?
For consciousness does not exist within consciousness;
and that which is non-existence is this perfection of wisdom.
For form, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations;
for consciousness is devoid of the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
That which is the absence of intrinsic nature is this perfection of wisdom;
for form has no intrinsic nature.
In the same way, feeling, perception, and mental formations [are without intrinsic nature];
for consciousness is indeed without intrinsic nature, and that which is the absence of intrinsic nature—
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is not the objective range of form;
nor is feeling, perception, or mental formations;
nor is consciousness the objective range of consciousness.
"Non-range," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, means that form does not perceive or see form.
And this non-perception and non-seeing of form is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not perceive or see;
and that which is the non-knowing and non-seeing of consciousness—
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form does not abandon the intrinsic nature of form;
nor do feeling, perception, or mental formations.
Consciousness does not abandon its own nature;
and that thorough knowledge of the absence of intrinsic nature is called the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form does not join with form, nor does it disjoin;
and that which is the non-joining of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
This non-disjunction is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form neither diminishes nor increases;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
consciousness neither diminishes nor increases.
And that which is the non-diminution and non-increase of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither defiled nor purified;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
consciousness is neither defiled nor purified.
That which is the absence of affliction and the absence of purification regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is called the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither of a pure nature nor of an impure nature; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are neither of a pure nature nor of an impure nature.
That which is neither the pure nature nor the impure nature of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form does not transmigrate nor does it descend;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness does not transmigrate nor does it descend.
That which is the non-transmigration and non-entrance of form, feeling, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither conjoined nor disjoined;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness neither joins nor disjoins.
That which is the non-joining and non-disjoining of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form neither passes away nor is it reborn;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness neither passes away nor is it reborn.
That which is the non-falling away and the non-arising of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither born nor does it die;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations;
consciousness is neither born nor does it die.
That which is the non-arising and non-dying of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form does not transmigrate, nor is it subject to transmigration;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness do not transmigrate, nor are they subject to transmigration.
That which is the non-transmigration and the nature of non-transmigration of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form does not diminish, nor is it subject to diminution;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness do not diminish, nor are they subject to diminution.
And that which is the inexhaustibility and the nature of inexhaustibility of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither subject to arising nor subject to cessation;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is neither subject to arising nor subject to cessation.
That which is the nature of non-arising and the nature of non-cessation of form, feeling, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither subject to arising nor subject to passing away;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is neither subject to arising nor subject to passing away.
That which is the non-arising nature and the imperishable nature of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither subject to transformation nor not subject to transformation;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
consciousness is neither subject to transformation nor not subject to transformation.
That which is neither the nature of transformation nor the nature of non-transformation of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither permanent nor impermanent;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent.
That which is neither permanence nor impermanence regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither pleasure nor pain; likewise, feeling, perception, and mental formations are neither;
and consciousness is neither pleasure nor pain.
That which is neither the state of pleasure nor the state of non-pleasure regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither self nor non-self; likewise, feeling, perception, and mental formations are neither self nor non-self;
and consciousness is neither self nor non-self.
That which is neither self-nature nor non-self-nature of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither subject to passion nor subject to dispassion;
and the same is true for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is neither of the nature of passion nor of the nature of dispassion.
That which is neither the state of passion nor the state of dispassion in regard to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither of the nature of hatred nor of the nature of non-hatred;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
consciousness is neither of the nature of hatred nor of the nature of non-hatred.
That which is neither the nature of aversion nor the nature of being free from aversion in regard to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither subject to delusion nor free from delusion;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
consciousness is neither subject to delusion nor free from delusion.
That which is neither the nature of delusion nor the nature of freedom from delusion regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no agent or instigator of form;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
There is no agent or instigator of consciousness.
That which is the state of being neither an agent nor a cause with respect to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no one who brings about or originates form;
likewise, there is none for feeling, perception, or mental formations;
nor is there anyone who brings about or originates consciousness.
That which is neither the raising up nor the causing to arise of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no knower or causer of knowledge regarding form;
likewise, there is none regarding feeling, perception, or mental formations;
nor is there any knower or causer of knowledge regarding consciousness.
That which is the state of being neither a knower nor a maker known with respect to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no one whatsoever who experiences or causes experience in regard to form;
likewise, there is none in regard to feeling, perception, or mental formations;
and there is no one whatsoever who experiences or causes experience in regard to consciousness.
And that which is the non-feeling and non-experiencing of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no one whatsoever who knows or sees form;
likewise, there is no one who knows or sees feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
That which is the non-knowing and non-seeing of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither annihilation nor permanence regarding form;
likewise, there is neither annihilation nor permanence regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
That which is the non-annihilation and non-eternality of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither an end nor an infinity for form;
likewise, there is neither an end nor an infinity for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
That which is neither the finitude nor the infinitude of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither the state of views nor the abandonment of the state of views; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are neither the state of views nor the abandonment of the state of views.
And that which is neither the state of views regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor the abandonment of the state of views— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is not craving, nor is it the abandonment of craving;
likewise, feeling, perception, and mental formations are not [craving].
Consciousness is not craving, nor is it the abandonment of craving.
That which is the absence of craving and the absence of the abandonment of craving regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form is neither wholesome nor unwholesome;
likewise, feeling, perception, and mental formations are not;
and consciousness is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
That which is neither the wholesomeness nor the unwholesomeness of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, neither going nor coming is perceived for form;
likewise, neither going nor coming is perceived for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
And where no coming or going of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is perceived—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither stability nor instability of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
That which is neither the stability nor the instability of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither a near shore nor a far shore for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
And that which is neither the state of being on this shore nor the state of being on the far shore of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither morality nor immorality.
That which is the state of neither morality nor immorality regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither attraction nor repulsion toward form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
And that which is the state of non-attraction and non-repulsion toward form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness neither give nor receive.
And that which is the non-giving and non-receiving of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither patience nor impatience.
And that which is neither patience nor impatience regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither vigor nor indolence.
That which is the absence of vigor and the absence of indolence in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no concentration of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor is there distractedness of mind.
That which is neither concentration nor distractedness of mind regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom.
That which is neither the state of wisdom nor the state of lack of wisdom regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there are neither perversions nor non-perversions.
And that which is neither the state of perversion nor the state of non-perversion regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither applications of mindfulness nor non-applications of mindfulness.
And that which is neither mindfulness nor non-mindfulness regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— (Vaidya 21)
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither right abandonments nor wrong abandonments.

And that which is neither the state of right abandonment nor the state of wrong abandonment regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither the bases of psychic power nor the immeasurables.
That which is the absence of both the state of being the bases of psychic power and the state of being the immeasurables in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the faculties, nor the powers, the factors of awakening, or the path;

and that which is the state of neither being faculties, nor powers, nor factors of awakening, nor the path for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither knowledge nor liberation.
That which is the non-existence of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and the absence of liberation in them— this is the perfection of wisdom.

For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither the meditations, liberations, concentrations, attainments, and superknowledges, nor are they the absence of superknowledges. That which is the state of neither being the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, nor being the superknowledges or the absence of superknowledges, regarding form, feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not emptiness, nor signlessness, nor wishlessness.
And that which is the absence of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
And that which is neither the state of being conditioned nor the state of being unconditioned in regard to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither attachment nor non-attachment.
That which is neither attached to nor unattached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither knowledge nor ignorance.
That which is the state of neither knowledge nor ignorance regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.

For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither conceiving, nor vibration, nor conceptual proliferation. And that which is the non-conceiving, non-vibration, and non-proliferation of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither perception nor non-perception.
And that which is the state of being neither perception nor non-perception regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither stilled nor un-stilled.
And that which is neither the stilling nor the non-stilling of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither the production nor the non-production of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
That which is neither the production nor the non-production of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— this is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching concerning the production and inclusion within the five aggregates is not the perfection of wisdom.
Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of that teaching concerning the production and inclusion within the five aggregates.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is an exposition included within the manifestation of the elements, the sense-bases, and dependent origination is not the perfection of wisdom.

Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-otherness, and the ultimate suchness of that exposition included within the manifestation of the elements, the sense-bases, and dependent origination.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is an exposition included within the production of the hindrances of perversion is not the perfection of wisdom.

Rather, the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of that exposition included within the production of the hindrances of perversion— [that is the perfection of wisdom].
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching included within the production of the thirty-six modes of craving is not the perfection of wisdom.
Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-otherness, and the ultimate suchness of that teaching included within the production of the thirty-six modes of craving.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching of the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments is not the perfection of wisdom.
Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-otherness, and the ultimate suchness of the teaching of the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching of the five superknowledges is not the perfection of wisdom;
rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of the teaching of those five superknowledges.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching on the manifestation included within all mundane conditioned phenomena— whether wholesome or unwholesome—
is not the perfection of wisdom. Rather, it is the suchness (*tathatā*) of that teaching, its non-falsity, its non-otherness, and its suchness as it truly is.
This is the perfection of wisdom.

For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching included within the actualization of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path is not the perfection of wisdom.

Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of that teaching included within the actualization of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching of the four noble truths is not the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, that which is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of the teaching on the four noble truths—
this is the perfection of wisdom.

For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching on the purity of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation is not the perfection of wisdom.

Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-otherness, and the ultimate suchness of that teaching on the purity of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching of those dharmas included in the unconditioned, supramundane, non-reliant, and untainted—

that is the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, that which is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the very suchness of the teaching of those dharmas included in the unconditioned, supramundane, non-reliant, and untainted— [that is the perfection of wisdom].
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching of the dharma of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and lack of volitional construction is not the perfection of wisdom.

Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of the teaching of the dharma of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and lack of volitional construction.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the teaching on knowledge, liberation, dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa is not the perfection of wisdom.
Rather, it is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of that teaching on knowledge, liberation, dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa.
This is the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is not included within form;
likewise, it is not included within feeling, perception, or mental formations.
The perfection of wisdom is not included within consciousness;
the perfection of wisdom is not included within earth, water, fire, wind, or space;
the perfection of wisdom is not included within the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm.
The perfection of wisdom is not included within conditioned or unconditioned phenomena;
the perfection of wisdom is not included within mundane or supramundane, tainted or untainted phenomena;
the perfection of wisdom is not included within wholesome or unwholesome phenomena.
The perfection of wisdom is neither included within the realm of sentient beings nor excluded from the realm of sentient beings;
yet the perfection of wisdom is also not separate from these phenomena.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is neither included within any dharma nor is it not included.
And that which is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of all dharmas— whether included or not included— is this perfection of wisdom.
“Suchness,” O Suvikrāntavikrāmin— of what is this a designation?
For these dharmas, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, are neither such as they are apprehended by foolish ordinary people,
nor are they otherwise.
Just as phenomena have been seen by the Tathāgatas, the disciples of the Tathāgatas, and the Bodhisattvas, so indeed are all those phenomena:
suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, and ultimate suchness.
Therefore it is called "suchness.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the teaching on the perfection of wisdom for bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this perfection of wisdom has not appeared for the sake of the diminution or the increase of any dharma;
nor for the sake of the conjunction or the disjunction of any dharma; nor for the sake of deficiency or fullness.
Whether for diminution or for accumulation,
for transition or for entry,
or for arising.
Whether for cessation,
or for affliction, or for purification,
or for proceeding, or for ceasing.
Whether for the sake of arising or for the sake of cessation,
whether for the sake of having characteristics or for the sake of being without characteristics,
whether for the sake of equality or for the sake of inequality.
Whether for the sake of conventional reality or ultimate reality,
for happiness or suffering,
or for permanence or impermanence.
Whether for the sake of purity or impurity,
for the sake of selfhood or selflessness,
or for the sake of truth or falsehood.

Then the Blessed One said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if a man who has seen a dream were to explain the nature of that dream, yet no such thing as the 'nature of a dream' exists at all."
For what reason?
Because even a dream does not exist; how much less, then, could there be an exposition of the intrinsic nature of a dream?
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is pointed out,
yet no intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom exists at all.
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a dream does not appear as a manifestation of any dharma whatsoever.
In the same way, the perfection of wisdom does not appear through the demonstration of any dharma whatsoever.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if a person who perceives an illusion were to give an exposition on the nature of illusions;
yet no such exposition on the nature of an illusion exists at all— how much less could there be a nature for the exposition of the nature of an illusion?
In the same way, the perfection of wisdom is taught,
yet no description of an intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom exists at all.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if an illusion were not present for the sake of bringing about any phenomenon whatsoever.
In the same way, the perfection of wisdom does not stand for the production of any dharma whatsoever.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if, for example, a person who perceives a reflection were to give an exposition on the intrinsic nature of that reflection;
yet no such intrinsic nature of a reflection exists at all— how then could there be an exposition on the intrinsic nature of a reflection?
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is taught,
yet no intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom exists;
how, then, could there be a teaching on the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom?
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a reflection does not appear by way of demonstrating any dharma whatsoever,
even so the perfection of wisdom does not appear by way of demonstrating any dharma whatsoever.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if, for example, a person who perceives a mirage were to point out that perception of a mirage,
yet no intrinsic nature whatsoever exists in that perception of a mirage.
How much less, then, could it have the nature of a vision of a mirage?
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is not pointed out,
nor does any description of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom exist.
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a mirage does not appear as an illustration of any dharma whatsoever,
even so the perfection of wisdom does not appear as an illustration of any dharma whatsoever.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if, for example, a person standing within the range of an echo hears the sound of that echo but does not perceive it [as a real entity];
yet when he himself repeats it, [he perceives it].
Then he hears that sound;
in this very way, he attains the words of the instruction on the perfection of wisdom for the purpose of hearing them,
yet he does not go to hear the instruction of any other dharma, except that when it is spoken, it is understood.
And it comes within the range of hearing.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if, for example, a person who sees a mass of foam were to describe the nature of that mass of foam,
yet the nature of the mass of foam is not perceived either internally or externally.
How much less, then, could there be the perception of its nature through description?
In this very way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is described,
yet the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is not perceived.
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a mass of foam does not possess the nature of being produced from any dharma,
even so the perfection of wisdom does not possess the nature of being produced from any dharma.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if, for example, a man who observes bubbles were to describe the nature of bubbles,
yet the nature of bubbles does not exist;
how then could there be a description of the nature of bubbles?
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is taught,
yet no intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom exists.
Just as, for example, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bubble does not appear with the intrinsic nature of being produced from any dharma whatsoever.
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom does not appear as having the nature of the production of any dharma whatsoever.
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a man searching for the core of a plantain tree does not find it, yet nevertheless performs his work with its leaves,
even so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the core of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not exist.
It provides an exposition of the perfection of wisdom and performs its function.
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a person might employ the conventional designation "space," yet no demonstration of space exists at all;
even so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the conventional designation "perfection of wisdom" is employed.
And it is not designated by way of any illustration;
just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, space is not designated,
nor is it designated by way of an illustration or by way of the perfection of any dharma whatsoever.
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is conventionally designated,
yet it is not conventionally designated by way of the demonstration or the completion of any dharma whatsoever.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as, for example, "shadow" and "sunlight" are conventionally designated,
yet they do not exist for the sake of establishing any dharma whatsoever,
even though they are perceived.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is precisely this perfection of wisdom that enters the sphere of conventional expression,
yet it does not enter the sphere of conventional expression through the demonstration of any dharma;
rather, it illuminates all dharmas.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if a refined jewel were present with a great radiance,
yet that radiance does not appear either internally or externally;
in the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the perfection of wisdom is present for the purpose of providing illumination.
And that radiance does not come within the range of vision, either internally or externally.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as, for example, when an oil lamp is burning, its flames do not remain steady even for a moment, yet they produce illumination; by that illumination, forms come into the range of vision.
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin,
the perfection of wisdom does not abide in any dharma whatsoever,
yet it brings illumination to all dharmas.
And by that illumination, all phenomena come to be seen as they truly are by the noble ones.

foot, vigor, laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, wisdom, lack of wisdom, mind, mentality, consciousness, immediate succession, death, rebirth, affliction, purification, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, the attainments, the superknowledges, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the contaminated, the uncontaminated, the mundane, the supramundane, the blameworthy, the blameless, the conditioned, the unconditioned, the determinate, and the indeterminate.

The perfection of wisdom is pure because it is purified of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair; the perfection of wisdom is pure because it is purified of perversions, hindrances, and views;
the perfection of wisdom is pure because it is purified of passion, hatred, and delusion.

The perfection of wisdom is utterly pure because it is pure of self, sentient being, life-force, nourisher, person, individual, human, man, agent, instigator, feeler, arouser, originator, knower, and seer.
The perfection of wisdom is utterly pure because it is pure of annihilation and permanence.
The perfection of wisdom is utterly pure because it is pure of finitude and infinity.
The perfection of wisdom is completely pure through the complete purity of the perfection of generosity;
it is completely pure through the complete purity of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom;
it is completely pure through the complete purity of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
The perfection of wisdom is completely pure;
it is completely pure through the complete purity of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
It is completely pure through the complete purity of the applications of mindfulness and the right efforts.
The perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of non-perversion;
the perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
the perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the superknowledges.
The perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the path;
the perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the stage of the śrāvaka;
the perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
The perfection of wisdom is pure because of the purity of the Buddha-ground;
the perfection of wisdom is pure because of the purity of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
the perfection of wisdom is pure because of the purity of the qualities of the Śrāvakas.
The perfection of wisdom is pure because of the purity of the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas;
the perfection of wisdom is pure because of the purity of the vision of the past, future, and present;
the perfection of wisdom is pure because of the purity of the vision of unattached knowledge.
The perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the desire realm, the purity of the form realm, and the purity of the formless realm.
The perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the earth element.
The perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the elements of fire, water, and air;
the perfection of wisdom is pure through the purity of the realm of sentient beings, the purity of the realm of phenomena, and the purity of the realm of space.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "It is marvelous, Blessed One, how far the perfection of wisdom is pure by its very nature.
The Blessed One said: "Śāradvatīputra, it is because of the purity of space that the perfection of wisdom is pure.
He said: "Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is formless and invisible."
[The Blessed One] said: "For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not appear through the perfection of form or by way of demonstration for any dharma whatsoever.
[Śāradvatīputra] said: "This perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, is unimpeded.
[The Blessed One] said: "For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma in which it might be impeded."
He said: "Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is uncreated.
He said: "Śāradvatīputra, because an agent is not apprehended.
He said: "Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom does not converge."
He said: "For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not come together with any dharma whatsoever.
He said: "O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is indefinable.
He said: "For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend any dharma by which it might be defined."
He said: "Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is uncommon.
[He said: "For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend any dharma by which it might be common.
He said: "Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is without characteristics."
He said: "Because its characteristics are unapprehendable, Śāradvatīputra.
He said: "Lord, this perfection of wisdom is non-manifestation.
He said: "By virtue of the non-apprehension of manifestation."
He said: "Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is infinite.
He replied: "Śāradvatīputra, it is an infinite perfection because form is infinite;
likewise, it is an infinite perfection because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are infinite."
This is an infinite perfection because of the infinity of perversions;
this is an infinite perfection because of the infinity of hindrances;

[and] because of the infinity of ignorance, the infinity of formative forces, the infinity of consciousness, the infinity of name-and-form, the infinity of the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair.
This is an infinite perfection:

because views are infinite, because passion, hatred, and delusion are infinite, because annihilationism and eternalism are infinite, and because the prior limit of existence is infinite— this is an infinite perfection.
Because it is infinite as far as the ultimate limit of the future, this perfection of wisdom is an infinite perfection.

Because giving is infinite, because ethical discipline is infinite, because patience is infinite, because vigor is infinite, because meditative concentration is infinite, and because wisdom is infinite, this perfection of wisdom—the perfection of wisdom—is an infinite perfection.

Because the applications of mindfulness are infinite, because the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are infinite, and because non-perversion is infinite, this is an infinite perfection.
This is an infinite perfection because of the infinity of the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments;
this is an infinite perfection because of the infinity of objective referents;
this is an infinite perfection because of the infinity of knowledge, liberation, and the vision and cognition of wisdom.
This is an infinite perfection because the stages of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the stage of the Buddha are infinite.
This is an infinite perfection because the qualities of the śrāvaka, the qualities of the pratyekabuddha, and the qualities of the Buddha are infinite.
This is an infinite perfection because self and sentient beings are infinite.
Because the realm of desire is infinite, this perfection is infinite; because the realm of form is infinite, this perfection is infinite;
because the formless realm is infinite, this perfection is infinite.
This is an infinite perfection because the superknowledges are infinite;
this is an infinite perfection because the hindrances are infinite;
this is an infinite perfection because the vision and knowledge of the past, future, and present are infinite.
Because it is unattached and infinite, because space is infinite, and because the realm of phenomena is infinite, this perfection is infinite.
For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, neither a beginning, nor a middle, nor an end of this perfection of wisdom is apprehended, nor has it been apprehended by anyone.
This perfection of wisdom, Śāradvatīputra, is infinite and boundless; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom.
Just as, Śāradvatīputra, the end of space is not apprehended, even so the end of the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended.
Because the earth element is infinite, Śāradvatīputra, the infinity of the perfection of wisdom should be seen.

The infinite nature of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to be understood through the infinitude of the water element, the infinitude of the fire element, the infinitude of the wind element, and the infinitude of the consciousness element.
For, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is to be realized as being without end, middle, or limit.
Indeed, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a particular place.
Śāradvatīputra, by way of the boundlessness of form, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood; and so on.
Likewise, Śāradvatīputra, by way of the boundlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood.

Śāradvatīputra, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of ignorance, the boundlessness of formative predispositions, the boundlessness of consciousness, the boundlessness of name-and-form and the six sense bases, and so on, up to the boundlessness of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Śāradvatīputra, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the perversions.
Śāradvatīputra, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the hindrances and the boundlessness of the various views.
Śāradvatīputra, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the self and the boundlessness of sentient beings.

Śāradvatīputra, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of generosity, the boundlessness of ethical discipline, the boundlessness of patience, the boundlessness of diligence, the boundlessness of meditative concentration, and the boundlessness of wisdom.
The infinity of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the infinity of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of miraculous power.

Śāradvatīputra, the infinity of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the infinity of the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and the attainments.
Śāradvatīputra, the infinity of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the infinity of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Śāradvatīputra, the limitlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the limitlessness of the superknowledges,

the limitlessness of liberation, and the limitlessness of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Śāradvatīputra, the limitlessness of the perfection of wisdom is [to be understood] through the limitlessness of the qualities of ordinary beings, the limitlessness of the qualities of śrāvakas, the limitlessness of the qualities of pratyekabuddhas, and the limitlessness of the qualities of buddhas.
It should be followed.

Śāradvatīputra, the limitlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be followed by way of the limitlessness of knowledge, the limitlessness of liberation, and the limitlessness of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Śāradvatīputra, it is called the "limitlessness of the perfection of wisdom" because no limit can be apprehended.
Because no end is perceived, it is called "infinite.
Śāradvatīputra, "infinite" is a term for the boundless.
Śāradvatīputra, one should understand the infinitude of all phenomena through the non-appropriation of a self.
“Śāradvatīputra, because space is infinite, all phenomena are to be understood as infinite and limitless.
When this was said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what kind of bodhisattvas have their sphere of activity within these phenomena?
The Blessed One replied: “Śāradvatīputra, those bodhisattvas who do not perceive even a phenomenon, let alone a non-phenomenon.”
They do not perceive even the path, let alone the non-path;
they do not perceive even ethical discipline, nor do they conceive of it, let alone immorality;
and they are unconfined within the entire triple world.
They are not confined within any state of existence, destiny, death, or rebirth;
they are unattached to body and life, let alone to external things;
and they have reached the further shore of the stream of saṃsāra.
And having crossed over the great ocean of existence,
and having emerged from the great battle,
Śāriputra, these are the domain and the range of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas regarding these dharmas.
Those noble persons who thoroughly understand that all objects are objectless, being thus unattached to any objects,
are like great lions.
They have not fallen into attachment toward any sense objects;
they are such noble beings (satpuruṣa).
They are entirely unstained by any sense objects.
They are unadulterated;
they have completely transcended all sense objects;
they are the great caravan leaders.
"Śāradvatīputra, those for whom there is both a domain and a range regarding these dharmas—
Śāradvatīputra, I do not see even a single bodhisattva in this assembly who lacks either a domain or a resolute conviction regarding these dharmas."
Or whoever might have longing or doubt regarding these dharmas—
Śāradvatīputra, this assembly is free from longing, free from doubt, and free from perplexity regarding these dharmas.
Śāradvatīputra, there is no uncertainty on the part of these bodhisattvas concerning these dharmas.
Śāradvatīputra, these true persons stand for the sake of all beings to eradicate doubt;
for, Śāradvatīputra, they are free from uncertainty regarding such dharmas as these, having completely transcended doubt.

Śāradvatīputra, those who in the future time, in the final age, shall hear this teaching of the Dharma, they too will become free from doubt regarding all phenomena, and they will be engaged in cutting through the doubts of all sentient beings.
And they will teach the Dharma free from doubt.
Śāradvatīputra, I do not say that beings with limited roots of merit have faith in these teachings;
nor is there even an opportunity for them in these teachings.

Nor is this wealth theirs; nor, Śāradvatīputra, will those beings be endowed with meager roots of virtue who even hear this teaching of the Dharma reach their ears, let alone those who will take it up, retain it, recite it, and master it.
They are destined for the qualities of a Buddha;
they have been prophesied by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
And in this way they will roar the lion’s roar, just as I now roar the lion’s roar—the unshakable roar, the roar of a Great Man, the roar of a Self-Existent One.

Those who, having generated absolute faith in these dharmas, will generate the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— for them too, those very same prophecies will come to pass. For what reason?
For those beings, Śāradvatīputra, who, having heard these profound dharmas, experience joy and give rise to gladness, are indeed rare to find.
And they have faith;
therefore, Śāradvatīputra, those beings who, having heard the profound teachings, give rise to the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, are the most difficult to find.
And they generate aspiration, being endowed with great roots of merit.
Śāradvatīputra, I do not say that those beings have set out upon the great saṃsāra who will even come within the range of hearing this teaching of the perfection of wisdom,
and having heard it—
They will recite it, they will have faith in it, and they will produce a sublime sense of joy and gladness;
they will generate a desire for these teachings even for the sake of hearing them again and again,
let alone for the purpose of teaching, reciting, or explaining them to others.
Śāradvatīputra, I prophesy that those who have not yet entered the fixed course and are not settled in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas will attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Śāradvatīputra, I do not perceive any room for beings possessed of inferior qualities to enter into the teachings before me.
Śāradvatīputra, this awakening of a Buddha is sublime.
For the most part, Śāradvatīputra, sentient beings have inferior inclinations, are endowed with inferior qualities, and have not performed wholesome deeds;
they are unskilled in such profound and stainless dharmas as these.

However, those who are noble beings, Śāradvatīputra—those with noble inclinations toward the Dharma, who have set out in the Mahāyāna, who have well accomplished their tasks, who are well-armored with the great armor, and who possess the most diverse meanings by way of the Great Path—[they are skilled in them].

They have set out upon a path that is not uneven, but straight, unobstructed, level, free from stumps and thorns, free from pits and precipices, pure, free from defilement, not crooked, and not devious—

those who have set out for the welfare of the world, for the happiness of the world, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
They are illuminators who serve as a ford for sentient beings;

they possess great compassion, are sympathetic toward their welfare, and desire their benefit, their happiness, and their security; they are present for the sake of providing a foundation of ease for all sentient beings.
Śāradvatīputra, for such beings—those bodhisattva mahāsattvas—this is great wealth. And it is those very mahāsattvas, Śāradvatīputra, who are the recipients of this jewel of the Dharma;
for them, this wealth is noble wealth.
For what reason?

Śāradvatīputra, for beings who have not performed meritorious deeds, who have not cultivated goodness, whose inclinations are inferior, and who lack faith, no inclination toward this sublime wealth arises.
And it was with this in mind, Śāradvatīputra, that I said: "Beings conform according to their elements; those with inferior inclinations associate with those who have inferior inclinations."
Those with noble inclinations [should associate] with those who have noble inclinations.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the range of activity of the perfection of wisdom?
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Śāradvatīputra: "Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom has an infinite range as its field of activity.
It is just as, for example, Śāradvatīputra, the element of wind has an infinite range as its field of activity."
In the same way, the perfection of wisdom has an infinite range of objects.
Just as, Śāradvatīputra, the element of wind has the element of space as its range of objects,
even so the perfection of wisdom has the element of space as its range of objects.
For example, Śāradvatīputra, just as the element of space and the element of wind are not seen anywhere, nor do they appear through the characteristic of the production of any dharma,
even so, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is not seen in any dharma whatsoever.
It does not appear with the characteristic of the production of any dharma whatsoever.
Śāradvatīputra, just as, for example, the element of space and the element of wind— being ungraspable and unestablished— do not enter into enumeration by way of color or signs,
even so, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom, being ungraspable and unestablished, [does not enter into enumeration].
It is designated or approached by means of some color-characteristic;

for example, Śāradvatīputra, just as the element of space and the element of wind do not approach through the perception of the perfection of any dharma, even so the perfection of wisdom does not approach through the perception of the perfection of any dharma.
He asked: "Blessed One, what is the characteristic of this perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāradvatīputra, this perfection of wisdom is without characteristics.
Śāradvatīputra, it is just as, for example, the element of space and the element of wind do not approach by way of the characteristic of the production of any dharma whatsoever."
In the same way, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not approach any dharma by way of the characteristic of its being fully established.
He asked: "Blessed One, what is the characteristic of this perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is indeed without characteristics."
Insofar as it does not exist by way of the characteristic of attachment—
just as, Śāradvatīputra, the element of space and the element of wind do not approach the characteristic of the perfect accomplishment of any dharma,
even so the perfection of wisdom does not approach the characteristic of the perfect accomplishment of any dharma.
For the perfection of wisdom, Śāradvatīputra, is without characteristics because it does not exist anywhere.
Just as, for example, Śāradvatīputra, the element of space does not adhere to anything, so too is the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, the perfection of wisdom does not adhere anywhere; therefore, it is called "having the characteristic of non-adherence. And yet, Śāradvatīputra, that which is non-adherent has no characteristic whatsoever.
Moreover, this is merely a conventional expression;
therefore it is said that "the perfection of wisdom has non-attachment as its characteristic.
Śāradvatīputra, that very characteristic of non-attachment is now being explained.
Furthermore, non-attachment has neither a defining characteristic nor a sign.
Śāradvatīputra, "non-attachment" is the thorough understanding of attachment;
it is the non-apprehension of attachment.
This is the thorough knowledge of attachment as it truly is; this is the thorough knowledge of the inversion of attachment.
For, Śāradvatīputra, no attachment is ever found within attachment.
Therefore, Śāradvatīputra, it is called the reality of non-attachment, which is the non-apprehension of attachment;
this perfection of wisdom is "non-attachment," and this is the teaching on the knowledge whose characteristic is non-attachment.
For all phenomena, Śāradvatīputra, have the characteristic of non-attachment;
whatever is the characteristic of a phenomenon, that is a non-characteristic.
For no dharma whatsoever has arisen for the sake of bringing about that characteristic;
and that wherein a characteristic is not found is called "the absence of characteristics" (alakṣaṇa).
And that which is without characteristics,
therein there is no attachment.
If there were a characteristic of dharmas, [there would be attachment].
There would have been attachment to all phenomena;
however, since they are "all phenomena," it is not as it is expressed.
That which has the characteristic of non-attachment cannot be expressed in words.
Why is that?
Because it is non-existent, it has the characteristic of non-attachment;
because it is secluded, it has the characteristic of non-attachment; because it is unapprehendable, it has the characteristic of non-attachment.
Śāradvatīputra, that dharma which has non-attachment as its characteristic does not appear by way of any demonstration,
nor by way of a vision of attachment.
Moreover, Śāradvatīputra, this demonstration of the characteristic of non-attachment has been made for the sake of sentient beings; for whatever is the characteristic of affliction,
that is a non-characteristic.
For defilement does not arise by way of characteristics;
rather, Śāradvatīputra, defilement arises by way of perversion.
And that which is perversion—
That is without characteristics.
That which is without characteristics is not a characteristic even by way of conventional expression.
This is without characteristics.
Even that which is purification, Śāradvatīputra, has no characteristic.
For what reason? Because,
son of Cārudattī, even affliction itself is without characteristics, let alone purification.
Śāradvatīputra, that thorough knowledge of affliction is as it truly is;
there is no affliction whatsoever in it.
Sentient beings, however, become afflicted because they are subject to perversion;
and that which is perverted is unreal. That which is unreal—how could there be the perfect establishment of reality therein?
Or rather, there is no characteristic.
That thorough knowledge of Śāradvatīputra is called purification.
Defilement itself is without characteristic,
let alone purification.
Both these, Śāradvatīputra, are phenomena without characteristic and are unestablished.
This is called "non-attachment.
All phenomena have non-attachment as their characteristic,
for indeed, attachment does not exist among all phenomena.
For, Śāradvatīputra, all foolish ordinary people become attached to things that have the characteristic of non-attachment.
This, Śāradvatīputra, is the teaching on the range of the knowledge of the characteristic of non-attachment of all phenomena.
And this, Śāradvatīputra, is the range of the perfection of wisdom.
For, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom has non-attachment as the characteristic of its cognitive range;
therefore it is called "the perfection of wisdom with an infinite range.
That which is non-attached—
It has as its range the domain of knowledge regarding infinite objects. "Range," Śāradvatīputra, is a designation for that which is without range.
For, Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is not cultivated by means of the characteristics of demonstrating a range.
"Object," Śāradvatīputra, is that which is not an object; this is the suchness and the reality of all phenomena. For all phenomena are indeed without objects.
Because they are without an object;
this very thorough knowledge of phenomena is called the "range of the object."
But it is not as it is said:
that this very absence of attachment anywhere through the thorough knowledge of all dharmas is called the characteristic of non-attachment.
Therefore, it is said that the perfection of wisdom has non-attachment as its characteristic.
Śāradvatīputra, among such dharmas as these, many companions are not found.
This is the exposition of the domain of the Tathāgata’s knowledge— namely, this indication, manifestation, and analysis of dharmas.

For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, among these dharmas there is no other companion whatsoever, except for disciples who have seen the truth, or irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas, or individuals endowed with right view who are not subject to regression.
Even for those, Śāradvatīputra, who are endowed with right view and who practice within these dharmas, doubt may still arise.
Śāradvatīputra, there is no doubt that both the body-witness and the bodhisattva who has attained patience [are included].
Śāradvatīputra, these dharmas are not the domain of foolish worldlings.
Śāradvatīputra, this exposition of the perfection of wisdom will not fall into the hands of beings with inferior inclinations.
Śāradvatīputra, those beings who come into the hands of this teaching of the perfection of wisdom will be endowed with completely pure roots of virtue and will have attended upon many Buddhas;
those beings will have planted roots of virtue and will possess noble intentions.

Those who have performed their service for the Blessed Buddhas, who have planted the seed of Buddhahood for the sake of awakening, who have embarked upon the Buddha-vehicle, who stand in the presence of the Blessed Buddhas, and who ask questions with proper reflection—
it is they into whose hands this teaching of the perfection of wisdom will fall;
they are close to attaining patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
Or they will have attained patient acceptance (kṣānti),
those into whose hands this exposition of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) shall come; and those who have received their prophecy (vyākṛta).
They will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, except for those who have [already] made a vow by the power of their own aspiration;
and those who have not yet been prophesied will swiftly receive a face-to-face prophecy.
Moreover, Śāradvatīputra, they should be considered as having already received their prediction through a face-to-face prediction.
For, Śāradvatīputra, this sūtra will not even come to the range of the ears of those beings whose roots of virtue are unripened,
let alone that they should obtain this sūtra, or cause it to be written, or honor it, or recite it, or meditate upon it.
Or that they would reveal it in detail to others—
such a thing is impossible.
Śāradvatīputra, those beings have fully ripened roots of virtue.
Those who shall hear, write, recite, or study this sūtra—
Śāradvatīputra, although this Dharma-discourse will come into the hands of those beings whose roots of merit are fully ripened— nevertheless [it will reach them].
Moreover, Śāradvatīputra, I declare to you, I announce to you:
having acquired these dharmas, that son of good family or daughter of good family— whether belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle or the Śrāvaka vehicle— should not be one of little zeal.

Śāradvatīputra, even if one is lazy, or full of torpor, or lacking clear comprehension, or with unestablished mindfulness, or with a distracted mind, or greedy for material things, or fickle, or talkative, or dull-witted, or impudent, or with ordinary faculties— nevertheless, the roots of virtue that have been performed do not fail to bear fruit.

Moreover, having attained these qualities, a bodhisattva should, to a still greater degree, cultivate heedfulness, vigor, enthusiasm, aspiration, non-laziness, restraint of the sense faculties, and lack of frivolity;
he should apply himself to the foundations of mindfulness and to great learning.
One who has initiated vigor must strive for the fulfillment of such qualities as these.
Śāradvatīputra, it is not the fruit of hearing such dharmas as these that a bodhisattva or one belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas would fall into negligence after having heard them.
He might place his trust [in them], or his zeal might decline, or his vigor might fail.
Or he might show laxity, or become full of ill-will;
thus this would not be fruitful.
Nor would such qualities as these have been heard by him.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, "hearing" is a designation for correct practice,
not for erroneous practice.
For indeed, Śāradvatīputra, this Dharma is not heard by one who has fallen into error.
Śāradvatīputra, you must be skilled in the meaning of what you have heard and established in its practice.
Śāradvatīputra, for those who have fallen into error, there is no conformable patience.
Śāradvatīputra, this is called "practice" in this Dharma: it is the practice of one who acts in accordance with the dharmas as they have been taught.
Śāradvatīputra, for a person endowed with patience and established in practice, there is no further rebirth in the states of woe.
One quickly attains realization in these teachings;
one should not place trust in merely inferior roots of virtue,
nor should one place trust in those who have not yet laid down their burden.
"Until one becomes fully perfected in these dharmas.
Śāradvatīputra, whoever has become fully perfected and trained in these dharmas, having attained patient endurance (*kṣānti*), would no longer perform karma that leads to rebirth in the lower realms;
nor would they ever again experience indolence or anything pertaining to the inferior portion.
Nor would he have any fear of turning back,
nor would he fall into laxity.
Why is that?
For, Śāradvatīputra, by him both affliction and purification are fully understood;
and he has seen, according to reality, that all phenomena have arisen from perversion and are unreal.
Thus seeing correctly, he becomes endowed with patience, gentle, and not dull-witted.

Established in the purity of ethical discipline and perfected in the restraint of conduct, sphere of activity, and behavior, Śāradvatīputra— even the gods long for such as these, let alone human beings;
such beings are desirable even to the gods, let alone to humans.
They become worthy of honor even by the gods, let alone by humans;
they become worthy of protection even by the gods, let alone by humans;
they become worthy of protection even by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, garuḍas, and gandharvas.
And they become eager for their protection, defense, and preservation.
The fourth chapter of the Noble Prajñāpāramitā, titled "The Chapter on Similes."
START Svp 5 (Vaidya 39) 5. The Fifth Chapter: Subhūti.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, why do you pass the time in silence?

Does it not occur to you to speak concerning the perfection of wisdom? Here the Teacher himself is present in person, and this assembly has become a worthy vessel for the teaching of the profound Dharma."
"Venerable Subhūti, this assembly is pure,
and it desires to hear the profound Dharma."

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable sir, I do not perceive that dharma concerning which it might occur to me to speak. Moreover, venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor the bodhisattva, nor even eloquence."
Nor is there that which appears, nor that by which it appears, nor that from which it appears.

Observing in this way, venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not perceive the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas— neither that which would manifest, nor that by which it would manifest, nor that from which it would manifest.
And as for that which might occur to his intuition:
"What shall I point out? What will occur to my intuition by starting from what?"
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this very non-verbalization, non-utterance, and non-designation is here the perfection of wisdom.
It is ineffable;
for indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom cannot be uttered or proclaimed.
Or even to express it;
such a response as this is the perfection of wisdom.

For indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is neither past, nor future, nor present. For indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom cannot be described as having the characteristic of the past, nor the characteristic of the future, nor the characteristic of the present.
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, this perfection of wisdom is without characteristics and beyond conventional discourse.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not perceive any characteristic of the perfection of wisdom by which the perfection of wisdom could be designated."
For indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that which is the past characteristic, the future characteristic, or the present characteristic of form is not the perfection of wisdom;
nor is that which is the past characteristic, the future characteristic, or the present characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness the perfection of wisdom.

And that which, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of the characteristics of past, future, and present form— that is the perfection of wisdom. And that which is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of past, future, and present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— [that is the perfection of wisdom].

This is the perfection of wisdom. And that, venerable Śāradvatīputra, which is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the ultimate suchness of the characteristics of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— past, future, and present— is impossible to designate, to proclaim, to express, or to explain away through vocal action.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, whoever enters into this teaching of the perfection of wisdom in such a manner understands the perfection of wisdom.
For, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not appear through the characteristic of a teaching of any dharma whatsoever.

It does not manifest by way of the characteristic of the demonstration of form; it does not manifest by way of the characteristic of the demonstration of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does it manifest by way of the characteristic of the demonstration of conditioned phenomena.
not by way of the characteristic of the teaching on dependent origination,
not by way of the characteristic of name-and-form,
and not by way of the characteristic of a self;
Neither by the characteristic of a sentient being,
nor by the characteristic of the realm of phenomena,
nor by the characteristic of conjunction.
not by way of the characteristic of dissociation,
not by way of the characteristic of cause, and not by way of the characteristic of condition;
Neither by the characteristic of suffering, nor by the characteristic of happiness,
nor by the characteristic of establishment, nor by the characteristic of non-establishment.
Neither by the characteristic of arising nor by the characteristic of passing away;
neither by the characteristic of affliction nor by the characteristic of purification;
nor by the characteristic of intrinsic nature.

It is manifested neither by way of the characteristic of conventional reality nor by way of the characteristic of ultimate reality; neither by way of the characteristic of truth nor by way of the characteristic of falsehood;
neither by way of the characteristic of transmigration nor by way of the characteristic of non-entry.
For what reason?
Because, venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is devoid of all characteristics;
it does not come within the range of vision of anyone as "this is the perfection of wisdom."
Or: "The perfection of wisdom is here," or "The perfection of wisdom is by means of this," or "The perfection of wisdom belongs to this."
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not perceive that dharma by which the perfection of wisdom could be pointed out.
For, venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not come as a demonstration of any dharma, nor does it perceive one.
For, venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not come as a demonstration of form."
It does not come within the range of perception of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it does not come within the range of perception of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
nor does it come within the range of perception of the elements or the sense bases.
It does not come within the range of demonstration of dependent origination, nor does it come within the range of demonstration of knowledge and liberation.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that wisdom which is supramundane and leads to penetration—
Even that perfection of wisdom does not come within the range of demonstration.

For example, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, just as no phenomenon comes within the range of demonstration of any other phenomenon, how can there be an utterance or an instruction regarding that very [perfection of wisdom]?
