Furthermore, venerable Śāradvatīputra, those who thus understand the principle of phenomena (dharmanaya) understand the teaching of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
For indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not exist for the purpose of demonstrating any dharma, nor for the purpose of pointing one out.
For indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom does not exist for the purpose of demonstrating form.
It is not manifested by the demonstration of form;
it is not manifested by the demonstration of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness,
nor by their non-demonstration.
It does not manifest through the demonstration of name-and-form,
nor through its illustration;
it does not manifest through the demonstration of affliction or purification.
It does not appear by way of demonstration,
nor does it appear by way of demonstrating dependent origination;
it does not appear by way of demonstration.
It does not appear through the manifestation of perversions, nor through their demonstration;
it does not belong to the realm of sentient beings.
It does not manifest through the manifestation of the self-element,
nor through its demonstration;
nor does it [manifest] through the earth element.
It does not appear through the manifestation of the elements of water, fire, or air,
nor through their demonstration;
it does not belong to the realm of desire.
It does not exist by way of being manifested from the realm of form, nor from the formless realm;
it is neither through demonstration nor through non-demonstration.
It does not appear through the manifestation or demonstration of generosity and stinginess, or ethical discipline and immorality;
it does not appear through the manifestation or demonstration of patience and malice, vigor and laziness, meditative concentration and distraction, or wisdom and foolishness.

It is not present through the manifestation of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the immeasurables, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the liberations, the concentrations, the attainments, or the superknowledges;
nor is it present through demonstration.
It is not present through the manifestation of the truths, the path, or the fruits.
It does not manifest by way of demonstration;
it does not manifest by way of demonstrating the stages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
it does not manifest by way of demonstration.
It is not the dharma of the śrāvakas, nor the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas,
nor the dharma of the bodhisattvas;
it does not manifest through the display of the dharmas of a buddha.
It does not appear through demonstration;
nor does it appear through the knowledge or non-knowledge of any dharma, nor through its manifestation or demonstration.
Nor does it appear through the manifestation or demonstration of the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of exhaustion, or the knowledge of cessation.
Nor is it present through the manifestation or the demonstration of nirvāṇa.
Just as, venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is not present through the manifestation or the demonstration of any dharma whatsoever, how shall I point out its conventional designation?
Moreover, venerable Śāradvatīputra, he who understands this teaching— that the perfection of wisdom does not appear through the demonstration or the illustration of any dharma—
he knows the perfection of wisdom and understands the teaching of the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom has not appeared for the sake of the conjunction or disjunction of any dharma.
Why is that?
For indeed, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom neither joins form nor disjoins it.
In this way, one neither joins nor disjoins feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
one neither joins nor disjoins dependent origination;
and one neither joins nor disjoins the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm.

He neither joins nor disjoins the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the wind element. He neither joins nor disjoins the realm of sentient beings, the realm of self, the realm of phenomena, or the realm of space. He neither joins nor disjoins generosity or stinginess, ethical discipline or immorality, patience or malice, vigor or laziness, meditative concentration or distraction, or wisdom or poor discernment.
It joins them neither together nor apart;

it joins them neither together nor apart as for the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the immeasurables, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the meditations, the liberations, the concentrations, the attainments, and the superknowledges;
it joins them neither together nor apart as for the path, the fruit of the path, suffering, the origin of suffering, or cessation.
It neither joins nor disjoins from the level of the śrāvaka, the level of the pratyekabuddha, the level of the bodhisattva, or the level of the Buddha.
It neither joins nor disjoins from the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of the Buddhas.
It neither joins nor disjoins from the equality of the three times—past, future, and present.
The knowledge of non-attachment and non-arising does not join nor does it disjoin, neither does it join nor disjoin from extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, just as a dharma does not exist for the sake of joining with or disjoining from any other dharma, how can there be an exposition of it?
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, seeing this purpose, I say this: I do not perceive any dharma that might occur to me,
by which it might occur to me, or from which it might occur to me.
"May it occur to me concerning this [topic]."
The fifth chapter, the Subhūti Chapter, in the Noble Perfection of Wisdom.
START Svp 6 (Vaidya 42) 6. The Sixth Chapter: On Conduct.

Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not practice in any dharma whatsoever.
For what reason? Because..."
For all phenomena, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, arise from perversion;
they are unreal, non-existent, false, and deceptive.
Just as it is, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when one courses in any phenomenon whatsoever, [it is likewise].
He courses in perversion;
coursing in perversion, he does not course in reality.
And, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva is not characterized by a course of perversion.
Or, it is characterized by unreal conduct;
nor does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom while practicing in error or in what is unreal. And that which is error is unreal.
Therein is no practice whatsoever;
therefore, a bodhisattva does not practice therein.
"Perversion," O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is false.
This has been grasped by foolish ordinary people; yet those phenomena are not as they are grasped, nor are they otherwise than how they have been grasped.
This is called "non-perversion" (aviparyāsa) here, meaning "that which is real.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in perversion or in that which is unreal.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva who speaks of what is real courses in non-perversion.
And where there is no error regarding reality, there is no practice whatsoever;
therefore it is said: "The non-practice is the bodhisattva practice."
For the bodhisattva practice, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the complete transcendence of all practices;
it cannot be demonstrated as "this is the bodhisattva practice" or "by means of this is the bodhisattva practice."
Whether as "the bodhisattva practice here" or "the bodhisattva practice from this," the bodhisattva practice is not manifested in such a way.

For it is for the sake of turning away from all [limited] conduct that Bodhisattvas practice the Bodhisattva conduct— turning away from the conduct of ordinary worldlings, turning away from the conduct of Śrāvakas, and turning away from the conduct of Pratyekabuddhas.
Even regarding those Buddha-qualities, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin,
Bodhisattvas do not practice them nor do they become attached to them, thinking, "These are the Bodhisattva-dharmas."
"Either these are your bodhisattva-qualities,
or by this means are they your bodhisattva-qualities,
or for this person are they your bodhisattva-qualities."
Even so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not course;
for all this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the practice of conceptualization.
A bodhisattva does not course in conceptualization, nor does he course in non-conceptualization.
For the conduct of a bodhisattva consists in the abandonment of all conceptual constructions.
"Conceptual construction," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the imagining of all phenomena; indeed, it is not possible to conceptually construct any phenomena.
For all phenomena are indeed unconstructed;
thus, whoever constructs a phenomenon,
he conceptualizes it.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a dharma is neither conceptualization nor discursive differentiation.
"Conceptualization," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is one extreme; "discursive differentiation" is the second extreme.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not course in the finite, nor does he course in the infinite;
he who courses neither in the finite nor in the infinite—
He does not perceive a middle.
Even while perceiving a middle, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, one who courses in the middle courses only in an extreme.
For there is no course whatsoever, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for a middle.
Or vision, or manifestation—
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, "the middle" is not even a designation for the noble eightfold path.
Moreover, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the noble eightfold path does not arise through the apprehension of any dharma,
nor through the contemplation of any dharma.
Moreover, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, at the time when a bodhisattva neither cultivates nor deconstructs any dharma, he is then said to have a path that is fully stilled.
Neither cultivating nor deconstructing any dharmas, having transcended cultivation, he attains the sameness of all dharmas.
By that equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*), even the notion of a "path" does not arise for him; how much less will he see a path?
"One whose path has been stilled," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a designation for an Arhat, a monk whose outflows are exhausted.
For what reason? Because that path has been fully understood; it is neither cultivated nor not cultivated. Therefore, it is called "fully understood."
Even the cultivation of discernment does not exist therein;
therefore it is called "discerned," for his cultivation has departed.
Therefore it is called "cultivation" (vibhāvanā).
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if cultivation or non-cultivation were to exist, that would be perceivable.
There would be no cultivation of this [perfection].

"Cultivation" (vibhāvanā), O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, means that in this [perfection] there is no cultivation; it is so called because cultivation has departed from it, or because its state of being (bhāva) has departed.
Therefore it is called "cultivation" (*vibhāvanā*), but not in the sense in which it is commonly expressed.
Why is that? For cultivation is beyond verbal expression.
This departure is the cultivation of non-apprehension.
What is departure?
It is the non-arising of error, which is the non-arising of that which has not come to be.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, perversion does not give rise to perversion;
this perversion is unarisen,
for there is no arising whatsoever therein.
If there were any arising therein, it would not be so called;
because it arises from what is unreal, it is therefore called "perversion" (viparyāsa).
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all phenomena have been fully awakened to by the bodhisattva as being non-perverted.
Why is that?
Because he has known that perversion is unreal.
In perversion, no perversion exists;
by which [knowledge] perversion is known as unreal,
in that perversion, no perversion exists.
Therefore, all phenomena have been fully awakened to as being non-erroneous;
and that which is the awakening to non-error,
therein there is no longer any error.
Where there is no perversion whatsoever, there is no practice whatsoever;
for, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, every practice is the arising of that very practice.
From conceptualization regarding conduct arises error;
however, the bodhisattva does not conceptualize regarding conduct.
Therefore, it is said that non-error abides together with that [conduct].
And he who is free from inversion does not course anywhere further;
therefore it is called "non-coursing" as the bodhisattva-course.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, ‘the practice’ (caryā) is that which does not course in any dharma, does not move about in them, and does not manifest the characteristic of practice;
this is called the bodhisattva practice. He who courses in this way—”
He courses in the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva practicing with form as an objective support does not practice in the perfection of wisdom;
practicing with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as an objective support, he does not practice in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
For by him all objective referents have been known as secluded;
and that which is seclusion,
therein there is no practice whatsoever.
Therefore it is called the "conduct of a bodhisattva.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva who courses in the objective support of the eye does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
nor does one who courses in the objective support of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind course in the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because he has known all objective referents to be unreal.
And whoever knows that all objective referents are unreal—
He does not course anywhere;
therefore it is called "non-coursing" as the bodhisattva-course.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva who courses with the objects of form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena is not coursing in the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because he has understood that all objective referents arise from cognitive distortion;
and whatever is cognitive distortion, [is itself empty].
That which is unreal has been fully understood;
by one who has fully understood the unreal nature of perversion, there is no longer any coursing in any object of perception whatsoever.
Therefore, it is called the "course of practice" (caryā) of a bodhisattva.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva who courses in the objective support of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-ālambana) does not course in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is that?
For by him all objective referents have been realized as being without objective referents;
and he by whom all objective referents have been realized as being without objective referents does not course in any objective referent whatsoever.
Therefore, it is called the "practice of a bodhisattva.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, [bodhisattvas mahāsattvas] do not [abide] in the objective support of sentient beings nor in the objective support of a self.
And they practice while coursing in the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because by them the notion of a "sentient being" and the notion of a "self" have been thoroughly understood—that this notion of a sentient being and this notion of a self are unreal.
And those by whom the unreal notion of a sentient being and the notion of a self have been understood do not course in any course whatsoever;
those who do not course in any course whatsoever—
And by that, practice is transcended;
therefore it is called "non-practice" as the bodhisattva practice.

O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those bodhisattvas who do not abide in the perception of a living being (*jīva*), or in the perception of a nourisher (*poṣa*), a person (*puruṣa*), an individual (*pudgala*), a human (*manuja*), a youth (*mānava*), an arouser (*utthāpaka*), an originator (*samutthāpaka*), a doer (*kāraka*), a causer (*kārayitṛ*), a feeler (*vedaka*), or a sufferer (*vedayitṛ*)—[they are the true bodhisattvas].
Those who course in the notion of a knower and a means of knowledge do not course in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because all notions have been thoroughly eliminated by them.
And those by whom all perceptions have been thoroughly analyzed no longer course within any perception whatsoever;
therefore it is said that "non-coursing" is the bodhisattva-course.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, Bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing through perversions, or views, or hindrances;
nor do they course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing in the objective supports of perversions, views, and hindrances.
Why is that?

For they have fully understood the objects of perversions, views, and hindrances; and that which is full understanding is non-practice. Therefore it is said: "The practice of a bodhisattva is non-practice."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, Bodhisattvas who course with dependent origination as their objective support do not course in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because they have fully understood dependent origination.
The objective support of dependent origination has been fully understood. As for that full understanding of dependent origination and its objective support,
therein there is no practice whatsoever.
Therefore, it is called the "conduct of a bodhisattva.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing with the realm of desire as their objective support;
nor do they course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing with the realms of form or formlessness as their objective support.
For what reason?
Because they have thoroughly cultivated the objects of perception belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
and that which is the cultivation of the objects of perception belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—
It has no practice whatsoever;
therefore it is called "non-practice" as the bodhisattva practice.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing with the objective supports of giving and stinginess, or ethical discipline and immorality.
For what reason?
Because they have fully understood the objective basis of generosity and stinginess, as well as ethical discipline and immorality;
and that which is the full understanding of the objective basis of generosity, stinginess, ethical discipline, and immorality—
In that [state], there is no practice whatsoever;
therefore it is called "non-practice" as the "practice of a bodhisattva.

For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing in the objective supports of patience and malice, vigor and indolence, meditative concentration and distraction, or wisdom and false wisdom.
For what reason?
Because they have fully understood all objective referents;
and that which is the full understanding of all objective referents—
In that regard, there is no practice whatsoever;
therefore it is called "non-practice" as the bodhisattva practice.

For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas who practice within the non-perverted right abandonments, the foundations of mindfulness, and the immeasurable objects do not practice in the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because they have realized that all objective referents are insubstantial; and this thorough knowledge of objective referents as being insubstantial—
For her there is no practice whatsoever;
therefore it is called "non-practice" the bodhisattva practice.

For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing in the objective supports of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditations, concentrations, and attainments.
For what reason?
Because they have fully cultivated the objects of the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the meditations, the concentrations, and the attainments; and as for that cultivation—
For her there is no practice whatsoever;
therefore it is called "non-practice" as the bodhisattva practice.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not practice in the perfection of wisdom while practicing with the objects of focus on suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
For what reason?
Because by them the objects of focus—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—have been fully cultivated; and as for that cultivation, it is...
In that there is no cultivation whatsoever, nor in it any further conduct;
therefore it is called "non-conduct" as the conduct of a bodhisattva.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, Bodhisattvas who course in the objective support of knowledge and liberation do not course in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because they have already eliminated the objective support of knowledge and liberation.
And as for that which is the elimination of conceptualization,
there is no practice whatsoever therein;
therefore it is said that "non-practice" is the "practice of a bodhisattva."

For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing in the objective support of non-arising, or the objective support of exhaustion, or the objective support of non-conditioning.
Why is that?
Because they have thoroughly eliminated the objective supports of non-arising, exhaustion, and non-conditioning.
And as for that which is the cultivation of non-conceptualization, there is no further practice therein; therefore it is said that "non-practice" is the "practice of a bodhisattva."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas who course by taking earth, water, fire, wind, and space as their objective supports do not course in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because they have already fully analyzed and abandoned those objective supports of earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
And since there is no practice whatsoever in that which is the elimination of conceptualization, it is therefore said that "non-practice" is the "practice of a bodhisattva."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, Bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing with the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas as their objective support.
Why is that?
Because they have already fully eliminated those objective supports of the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
And as for that which is the elimination of conceptualization,
there is no practice whatsoever therein;
therefore it is said that "non-practice" is the "practice of a bodhisattva."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing with the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as their objective support.
Why is that?
Because they have thoroughly eliminated those objective supports consisting of the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
And as for that which is the elimination of conceptualization,
therein there is no practice whatsoever;
therefore it is said that "non-practice" is the "practice of a bodhisattva."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, Bodhisattvas who course with nirvāṇa as their objective support do not course in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because they have fully understood the objective support of nirvāṇa.
And as for that thorough knowledge,
there is no practice whatsoever therein;
therefore it is said that "non-practice" is the "bodhisattva practice."
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas do not course in the perfection of wisdom while coursing with the purification of the marks as their objective support,
nor while coursing with the purification of the buddha-field as their objective support, nor while coursing with the excellence of the śrāvakas as their objective support.
Those who course with the perfection of a bodhisattva as their objective do not course in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because they have eliminated the objective support of the purity of marks.
The objective support of the purification of the buddha-field,
the objective support of the excellence of the śrāvakas, and the objective support of the excellence of the bodhisattvas.
And since there is no practice whatsoever in that which is the elimination [of conceptualization], it is therefore called "non-practice" the practice of a bodhisattva.
Moving in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, bodhisattvas move in the perfection of wisdom.

This is the practice of the thorough comprehension of all objects of focus and the practice of the elimination of all objects of focus for a bodhisattva moving in the perfection of wisdom; that is to say, it is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not practice even in the purification of the objective support of form;
likewise, he does not practice even in the purification of the objective supports of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
For what reason?
For by him the objective support of form has been fully understood as naturally pure;
likewise, the objective supports of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have been fully understood.
Such is this practice.
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.

Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not practice for the purification of the objective field of the eye, nor does he practice for the purification of the objective fields of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
For what reason?
Because he has fully understood that even the objects of the mind are pure by nature.
Such is this practice.
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Moving in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva does not even practice for the sake of the purification of the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
For what reason?
For by him all objects of phenomena have been thoroughly understood as being pure by nature;
such conduct is the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva does not even practice in the purification of the objective support of name-and-form.
Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the objective support of name-and-form is pure by its very nature.
Such practice as this is the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not even practice for the sake of the purification of the objective referents of self and sentient beings.
For what reason?
Because he has fully understood the nature of the objective basis of self and sentient beings;
such is his conduct.
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.

Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not [perceive] a living being, a creature, a person, an agent, a causer, an arouser, an instigator, an experiencer, an feeler, or a seer—even in the purification of the objective support.
And for what reason?

For by him, that which is naturally pure has been fully understood as the basis for the notions of a living being, a state of existence, a person, an agent, an instigator, an arouser, an originator, an experiencer, one who causes experience, and a seer.
Such a practice is the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not even practice for the purification of the objects of inverted views.
Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the objects of inverted views are pure by nature.
Such practice as this is the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva does not even practice for the purification of the objects of the hindrances.
For what reason?
Because the object of the hindrances is thoroughly understood as being pure by nature.
Moving in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not even course in the purity of the object of dependent origination.
For what reason?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the objective support of dependent origination is pure by nature.
Moving in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not even course in the purification of the objective supports of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
For what reason?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the objective supports of the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm are by nature pure.
Moving in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva does not even practice for the sake of the purity of the objective supports of generosity and stinginess, or ethical discipline and immorality.
For what reason?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the basis of giving and stinginess, as well as ethical discipline and immorality, is by nature pure.

Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not practice even in the purification of the objects of focus for patience and malice, vigor and indolence, meditative concentration and distraction, or wisdom and faulty wisdom.
Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the objects of focus for patience and malice, vigor and indolence, meditative concentration and distraction, and wisdom and faulty wisdom are pure by nature.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not practice even within the purity of objects belonging to the past, future, or present.
Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly understood that objects of the past, future, and present are pure by their very nature.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not even practice for the sake of the purification of non-attachment and non-obstruction.
Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the object of non-attachment is pure by its very nature.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not even practice for the purification of the objects of the superknowledges.
Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the objects of the superknowledges are pure by nature.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva does not even practice in the purification of the objective support of omniscience.
Why is that?
Because he has thoroughly understood that the objective support of omniscience is pure by its very nature.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva practicing in this way practices the perfection of wisdom,
in that he does not practice in any purification of objective referents.
For what reason?
Because all objective referents are pure by nature,
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the natural purity of all objective referents for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not perceive "this is form," nor does he perceive "by means of this is form," nor does he perceive "of this is form."
He does not perceive "form" as being from this;
thus, not perceiving form, he neither elevates nor deprecates form, and he neither produces nor ceases form.
He does not course in form, nor does he course about it;
he does not course in the objective support of form, nor does he course about it.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when he courses in this way, a bodhisattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, one does not perceive: "these are feeling, perception, and mental formations; this is consciousness," nor does one perceive: "by means of this, there is consciousness."
He does not perceive "consciousness belongs to this," nor does he perceive "consciousness arises from this.
Thus, not perceiving consciousness in such a way, he neither elevates nor deprecates consciousness.
It does not produce consciousness nor does it cease it;
it does not course in consciousness nor does it course apart from it; it does not course in the objective referent of consciousness nor does it course apart from it.
In this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices in this way, he does not practice with the thought that form is past, nor does he practice with the thought that form is future, nor does he practice with the thought that form is present.
In this way, one does not course in the idea that feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness are past, nor that they are future.
Nor is it the present.
One does not course in the notion that form is the self, nor does one course in the notion that form belongs to the self;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He does not practice with the thought that consciousness is the self, nor does he practice with the thought that consciousness belongs to the self;
he does not practice with the thought that form is suffering.
In this way, one does not practice with the thought that "feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are suffering," nor does one practice with the thought that "form belongs to me, or to others."

In this way, he does not practice with the thought, "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are mine, or they belong to others. Suvikrāntavikrāmin, practicing in this manner, a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice in the arising of form,
nor does he practice in the cessation of form.
He does not practice with the thought that form is profound; he does not practice with the thought that form is superficial; he does not practice with the thought that form is empty.
He does not course in the thought that form is non-empty; he does not course in the thought that form has signs; he does not course in the thought that form is signless.
He does not practice with the thought that form is with aspiration;
he does not practice with the thought that form is without aspiration; he does not practice with the thought that form is conditioned.
He does not practice with the thought that form is non-conditioning;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He does not practice regarding the arising of consciousness.
He does not course in the cessation of consciousness;
he does not course in the thought that "consciousness is profound," nor does he course in the thought that "consciousness is shallow."

He does not practice with the thought that consciousness is empty; he does not practice with the thought that consciousness is non-empty; he does not practice with the thought that consciousness has signs.
He does not practice with the thought that consciousness is signless;
he does not practice with the thought that consciousness is wishless;
he does not practice with the thought that consciousness is not wishless.
He does not practice with the thought "consciousness is conditioned," nor does he practice with the thought "consciousness is unconditioned.
For what reason?
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all these are conceited, flickering, and conceptual proliferations belonging to craving.
To think "I am practicing" is a flickering; to think "I am practicing here" is a conceptual proliferation.
"I move by means of this" is a form of craving; "I move within this" is a form of conceit.

In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when Bodhisattvas recognize all these as conceits, stirrings, and conceptual proliferations belonging to craving, they do not conceive of any dharma whatsoever, because they have uprooted all ignorance.
Being without conceit, they do not move anywhere, nor do they cling anywhere;
being without clinging, without union, and without disunion, they do not give rise to anything anywhere.
They do not give rise to them;
this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the eradication of all conceits for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices in this way in the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice with the thought that "form is permanent" or "form is impermanent";
he does not practice with the thought that "form is empty" or "form is non-empty";
he does not practice with the thought that "form is like an illusion."
He does not course in the thought that form is like a dream; he does not course in the thought that form is like an optical illusion; he does not course in the thought that form is like an echo.
In the same way, one does not course in the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are permanent or impermanent;
nor does one course in the notion that consciousness is empty or non-empty.
He does not practice with the thought that consciousness is like an illusion; he does not practice with the thought that consciousness is like a dream;
he does not practice with the thought that consciousness is like a reflection.
One does not practice with the thought that "consciousness is like an echo.
Why is that?
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all these are merely conceptualized, deliberated upon, and practiced or contemplated as such.

In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva, having understood all these thoughts, reflections, and deliberations, practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of uprooting all conduct and for the sake of fully comprehending all conduct.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the exposition of the bodhisattva’s all-conduct.
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, this practice of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva is inconceivable.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Suvikrāntavikrāmin.
Because form is inconceivable, this practice of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva is inconceivable."
Thus, due to the inconceivability of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable;
due to the inconceivability of name-and-form, this practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable;
and due to the inconceivability of dependent origination and the inconceivability of affliction, this practice of the Bodhisattva’s [perfection of wisdom] is inconceivable. (Vaidya 49)
The practice of the perfection of wisdom:
this practice of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva is inconceivable because the ripening of karma is inconceivable; it is inconceivable because its essence is inconceivable.
This [practice of a bodhisattva] is inconceivable.

This practice of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva is inconceivable because of the inconceivability of perversions; this practice of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva is inconceivable because of the inconceivability of views.
Because the desire realm is inconceivable,
the form realm is inconceivable,
and the formless realm is inconceivable, this practice of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable.
Through the inconceivability of the self,
the inconceivability of sentient beings,
and the inconceivability of giving.
Through the inconceivability of stinginess, the inconceivability of ethical discipline,
and the inconceivability of immorality.
through the inconceivability of patience, the inconceivability of malice,
and the inconceivability of vigor;
due to the inconceivability of laziness, the inconceivability of meditative concentration, the inconceivability of distraction,
and the inconceivability of wisdom;
Because of the inconceivability of faulty wisdom, the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom is inconceivable;
because of the inconceivability of passion, hatred, and delusion, this bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom is inconceivable;

because of the inconceivability of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the absence of perversions, and the bases of psychic power, this bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom is inconceivable.
This practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable due to the inconceivability of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, and attainments;
this practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable due to the inconceivability of the [five] destinies;
this practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable due to the inconceivability of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

This practice of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable because of the inconceivability of knowledge and liberation; it is inconceivable because of the inconceivability of the cognition of exhaustion, the cognition of non-arising, and the cognition of formative activity.
This practice of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable because of the inconceivability of the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
Because the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are inconceivable, this practice of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable;
because the superknowledges are inconceivable,
and because the knowledge of the past, future, and present is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom is inconceivable.

This practice of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is inconceivable because of the inconceivability of unattached knowledge, the inconceivability of nirvāṇa, and the inconceivability of the buddha-qualities.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the practice of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva does not produce a mind;
therefore it is called "inconceivable."
“O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, ‘the arising of the mind’—this is a perversion. O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, ‘the mind is born from the mind’—this is a negation of the mind.
For, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is the intrinsic nature of the mind does not arise, nor is it ever born.”
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a mind associated with perversion arises;
therein, even the mind is exposed,
and that by which it arises through perversion is utterly exposed.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, foolish ordinary people do not understand that the mind is open;
for that in which it arises is open,
and that by which it arises is also open.
Not understanding the solitude of the mind and not understanding the solitude of objective referents, they become attached, thinking: "I am the mind; the mind is mine."
Thinking "the mind is this" or "the mind comes from that," they become attached to the mind and become attached to it as being either wholesome or unwholesome.
They adhere to the notion that it is unwholesome;
they adhere to the notion that it is pleasant, or they adhere to the notion that it is painful.
They adhere to the view of annihilationism; they adhere to the view of eternalism; they adhere to dogmatic views.
They adhere to the notion of "hindrances";
they adhere to the notions of "generosity" and "miserliness," "virtue" and "immorality";
and they adhere to the notions of the "dharma-realm," the "desire realm," the "form realm," and the "formless realm."
They adhere to dependent origination;
they adhere to name-and-form;
they adhere to passion, hatred, and delusion.
They adhere to envy and avarice; they adhere to the conceit "I am";
they adhere to suffering.
They adhere to the notion of "origination";
they adhere to the notion of "cessation";
they adhere to the notion of "the path."
They adhere to the foundations of mindfulness;
they adhere to the right efforts, the non-perversions, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment;
and they also adhere to the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
They adhere to the notions of non-arising, exhaustion, and lack of volitional construction;
they adhere to the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
and they also adhere to the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
They adhere to the path;
they also adhere to the supernormal powers;
they even adhere to nirvana.
They also adhere to the wisdom of a Buddha;
they also adhere to the [physical] marks;
they also adhere to the perfection of a Pratyekabuddha.
They also become attached even to the perfection of a bodhisattva.

In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva perceives that these kinds of attachments in sentient beings arise from a mind of perversion, he does not give rise to a mind of perversion toward anything at all.
Why is that?
Because the perfection of wisdom is free from the mind.
And as for that luminosity of the nature of the mind and its natural purity, therein there is no arising of the mind at all.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is only when there is an objective referent (*ālambana*) that foolish ordinary beings give rise to the mind.
In that regard, the bodhisattva, while cognizing the object of perception, also cognizes the arising of the mind, [inquiring]: "From what does the mind arise?
He examines it thus: "This mind is luminous by nature.
It occurs to him: "The mind arises in dependence upon an object of perception."
Having fully understood that objective support, he neither produces nor ceases the mind.
His mind becomes luminous, unafflicted, lovely, and utterly pure.
Abiding in the non-arising of the mind, he neither produces nor ceases any dharma whatsoever.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the thorough knowledge of the non-arising of the mind for one who courses in the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva who courses in this way courses in the perfection of wisdom.

As he practices in this way, it does not occur to him: "I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," "I am practicing in this perfection of wisdom," or "I am practicing by means of this perfection of wisdom."
"I course in this perfection of wisdom"—
if, moreover, he perceives: "This is the perfection of wisdom," or "By means of this perfection of wisdom," [he courses in it].
Or, thinking "this is the perfection of wisdom," he does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
furthermore, when he neither perceives nor apprehends even that perfection of wisdom, he does not course [with the thought], "I am coursing in the perfection of wisdom."
He courses in the perfection of wisdom.

When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin addressed the Blessed One as follows: "This practice, Blessed One, is unsurpassed for a bodhisattva—namely, the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
This practice, Blessed One, is luminous for a bodhisattva—namely, the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
This practice, Blessed One, is supreme for a bodhisattva—namely, the practice of the perfection of wisdom."

"O Blessed One, this practice of a bodhisattva— namely, the practice of the perfection of wisdom— is most wonderful! O Blessed One, this practice of a bodhisattva cannot be entered by Māra, nor by the retinues of Māra, nor by any others who practice with signs, who practice with apprehension, or who hold views of a self, views of a sentient being, or views of a living soul."

Whether by those with views of a person, views of existence, views of non-existence, views of annihilation, or views of permanence; by those with views of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), views of the aggregates, views of the elements, or views of the sense-bases; by those with views of the Buddha, views of the Dharma, views of the Saṅgha, or views of Nirvāṇa;
whether they are those who possess correct discernment, or those who are conceited, or those whose conduct is dominated by passion, hatred, or delusion—(Vaidya 51)
It cannot be overcome by those whose conduct is characterized by perversion or who have set out upon bypaths and wrong paths.
Blessed One, this practice of the Bodhisattva, namely the practice of the perfection of wisdom, is a practice for the exaltation of the entire world.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "It is so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is so.

This conduct of a bodhisattva is one not entered upon by Māra, nor by the sons of gods belonging to Māra’s host, nor by the assembly of Māra; it is even unassailable by those who hold a view of nirvāṇa or those who are attached to nirvāṇa, and it is unassailable by all foolish ordinary people."
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this conduct of the bodhisattvas is not the conduct of foolish ordinary people,
nor is it the conduct of those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas who are either in training or beyond training.
Nor does it belong to those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if this practice were that of those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, there would be no designation for them as "belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle" or "belonging to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle."
If they had been bodhisattvas,
they too would have become Tathāgatas who have attained the four grounds of self-confidence;
however, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, since this practice does not belong to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle nor to those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, [it is the practice of the bodhisattvas].
Therefore, they do not enter into the reckoning of Bodhisattvas,
nor do they become Tathāgatas who have attained the four grounds of self-confidence.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the ground of self-confidence within the Dharma.
This is not the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when Bodhisattvas practice in this way, they quickly attain the four grounds of self-confidence,
even while they have not yet fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— both by the power of their vow and by the power of the empowerment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas do not possess the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*),
nor does the Tathāgata bestow the four grounds of self-confidence upon them.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the stage of the bodhisattva, in which the four grounds of self-confidence are attained through the power of one's vow.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, while practicing in the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattvas attain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
What are the four?

That is to say: the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
Endowed with these four analytical knowledges, even though they have not yet attained full awakening, they acquire the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) by the power of their vows.

The Tathāgatas, likewise, recognizing that they are endowed with roots of virtue and recognizing that they have reached the stage of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitābhūmi*), empower them with the four grounds of self-confidence.

Therefore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and who wishes to quickly become skilled in the four grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya) should train in and practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he thoroughly investigates the cause, the origin, the disappearance, and the cessation of all phenomena;
there is no phenomenon whatsoever that he does not apply to the perfection of wisdom.
He thoroughly understands the characteristics of the cause, origin, cessation, and path of all phenomena.
Thoroughly understanding those characteristics of cause, origin, cessation, and path, he neither brings form into being nor causes it to cease;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One does not cultivate nor does one eliminate consciousness; one does not cultivate nor does one eliminate name-and-form;
one does not cultivate nor does one eliminate affliction and purification.
He does not cultivate nor does he eliminate the perversions, views, and hindrances;
he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate passion, hatred, and delusion;
he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm.
He does not cultivate nor does he eliminate the realm of sentient beings, nor the realm of self; he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate the view of annihilation, nor the view of eternalism;
he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate generosity or stinginess.
He does not cultivate nor does he eliminate either morality or immorality; he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate either patience or malice;
he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate either vigor or laziness, meditative concentration or distraction, or wisdom or lack of wisdom.

He does not cultivate nor does he eliminate the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the non-perversions, and the bases of psychic power; he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the concentrations, and the meditative attainments;
he does not cultivate nor does he eliminate dependent origination.

He neither cultivates nor eliminates suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; he neither cultivates nor eliminates the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of exhaustion, or the knowledge of conditioned formation; he neither cultivates nor eliminates the stage of ordinary beings.
He neither cultivates nor eliminates the stage of the śrāvaka, nor the stage of the pratyekabuddha;
he neither cultivates nor eliminates the dharmas of ordinary persons, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, [nor the dharmas of bodhisattvas and the dharmas of buddhas].
One neither cultivates nor eliminates calm abiding (śamatha) nor insight (vidarśanā); one neither cultivates nor eliminates nirvāṇa;
one neither cultivates nor eliminates the knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present.
He does not cultivate attachment, nor does he eliminate it; he does not cultivate non-attachment, nor does he eliminate it;
he does not cultivate the wisdom of a Buddha, nor does he eliminate it.
He does not cultivate nor does he eliminate the fearlessnesses of a Buddha.
Why is that?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not to be cultivated.

The name-and-form, the perversions, the views, the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the non-perversions, the immeasurables, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the meditative concentrations, the attainments, the superknowledges, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-formation are not to be cultivated;
the stage of ordinary beings is not to be cultivated; and the stages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are not to be cultivated.
The dharmas of ordinary persons, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are non-existent; nirvāṇa is non-existent;
and the knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present are non-existent.
The vision of unattached knowledge is impossible to cultivate; the vision of unimpeded knowledge is impossible to cultivate; the knowledge of a perfectly awakened Buddha is impossible to cultivate.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no such thing as the perfect establishment of any entity;
for all these conventional expressions are indeed unreal.
There is no intrinsic nature whatsoever here;
for all phenomena, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, have non-existence as their intrinsic nature,
being unarisen and unproduced.
For what reason?
Because whatever is a perversion is unreal;
all phenomena arise from perversion.
For whatever is a perversion is non-existence;
indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all phenomena are devoid of existence. Existence is not apprehended because of the absence of intrinsic nature.
"Non-existence," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, means that which has not come to be;
it is unproduced, and for that reason it is called "non-existence."
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is an illumination of the non-existent, namely "non-existence.
And that which is non-existence,
therein there is neither cultivation nor elimination.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is because they are arisen from perversion that sentient beings both cultivate and deconstruct;
yet therein there is nothing at all to be cultivated.
Why is that?
For all phenomena, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
they are devoid of being because of the non-existence of any substantial entity.
Therein, nothing at all is to be cultivated.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, at whatever time a bodhisattva, dwelling thus as one who contemplates phenomena within phenomena while practicing the perfection of wisdom, neither cultivates nor deconstructs any phenomenon whatsoever—

this is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices and dwells in this way, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reaches fulfillment.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, no thought arises that is associated with the sign of form;
nor [a thought] associated with feeling, nor with perception.
There is no formative activity;
no mind arises conditioned by association with consciousness;
no mind arises accompanied by stubbornness.
A mind accompanied by ill will does not arise; a mind accompanied by stinginess does not arise;
a mind accompanied by affliction does not arise.
A mind accompanied by laziness does not arise;
a mind accompanied by distraction does not arise;
a mind accompanied by faulty wisdom does not arise.
A mind accompanied by sensual desire does not arise;
a mind accompanied by attachment to the objective support of form does not arise;
a mind accompanied by covetousness does not arise.
A mind accompanied by malicious speech does not arise;
a mind accompanied by wrong view does not arise;
a mind accompanied by attachment to enjoyments does not arise.
A mind accompanied by attachment to power does not arise; a mind accompanied by attachment to rebirth in a great family does not arise;
a mind accompanied by attachment to rebirth as a deity does not arise.
A mind accompanied by attachment to the desire realm does not arise;
a mind accompanied by attachment to the form or formless realms does not arise;
and a mind directed toward the level of a śrāvaka does not arise.
The mind does not arise on the level of a pratyekabuddha;
nor does a mind arise accompanied by attachment or clinging to the conduct of a bodhisattva;
nor, even to the slightest degree, does a mind arise accompanied by the view of hindrances.
Endowed with this purity of mind, he pervades sentient beings with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
yet he has eliminated the perception of a "sentient being" and does not abide in the perception of a "sentient being."
Nor does he become attached to these four divine abodes;
rather, he becomes wise and endowed with skill in means.
For one who is thus endowed with these qualities and practices the perfection of wisdom, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom quickly reaches fulfillment.
Thus cultivating the perfection of wisdom, he does not approach form, nor does he grasp it;
he does not approach feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness, nor does he grasp them.
He does not approach nor grasp at perversions, hindrances, or views;
he does not approach nor grasp at the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm;
he does not approach nor grasp at annihilationism or eternalism.
He does not approach dependent origination, nor does he grasp it;
he does not approach the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind, nor does he grasp them;
he does not approach passion, hatred, or delusion, nor does he grasp them.
He does not approach nor does he grasp at giving and stinginess, or morality and immorality;

he does not approach nor does he grasp at patience and malice, vigor and laziness, meditative concentration and distraction, or wisdom and false wisdom; he does not approach nor does he grasp at the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the non-perversions, the immeasurables, or the bases of miraculous power.
He does not approach nor grasp the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, meditative absorptions, liberations, or attainments;
he does not approach nor grasp the superknowledges;
he does not approach nor grasp suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.
He does not approach nor grasp the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of destruction, or the knowledge of conditioned formation;
he does not approach nor grasp the realm of self, the realm of sentient beings, or the realm of phenomena;
he does not approach nor grasp the stage of ordinary persons, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or perfectly enlightened buddhas.
He does not approach nor grasp the dharmas of ordinary persons, nor the dharmas of śrāvakas, nor the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas;
he does not approach nor grasp the knowledge and vision of the past, future, or present.
He does not approach, nor does he grasp, the vision of unattached knowledge; he does not approach, nor does he grasp, the Buddha-knowledge, powers, and grounds of self-confidence;
he does not approach, nor does he grasp, the hindrances.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all dharmas are indeed unapproached and unappropriated; they have not been approached by anyone.
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no dharma whatsoever to be grasped, nor has anything ever been grasped by anyone.
Why is that?
Because herein there is nothing at all to be grasped.
Nor is it something to be grasped.
For what reason?
Because, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all phenomena are essence-less, being like an illusion.
For all phenomena are masteries because their core essence is unapprehendable;
for all phenomena are like reflections because they are ungraspable;
for all phenomena are empty because they lack intrinsic nature.
For all phenomena are like a mass of foam, because they cannot withstand being crushed;
all phenomena are like bubbles, by virtue of their arising, breaking, and dissolving;
all phenomena are like a mirage, by virtue of their arising from perversion.
For all phenomena are like the core of a plantain tree, by virtue of their lack of substantiality;
they are like the moon reflected in water, by virtue of their ungraspability; they are like the colors of a rainbow, by virtue of being unreal conceptualizations;
and they are devoid of agency, by virtue of their non-arising.
For all phenomena are like an empty fist, because their characteristic nature is insubstantial.
In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva thus thoroughly observes all phenomena, he does not approach any phenomenon, does not grasp it, and does not dwell upon it.
He does not abide in attachment.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the faith in all dharmas, the state of non-abiding, the state of non-attachment, and the state of non-clinging of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
For a bodhisattva practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reaches fulfillment.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva training in this way does not train in form,
nor does he train for the sake of transcending form;
nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations.
He does not train in consciousness, nor does he train for the sake of transcending consciousness;
he does not train in the arising of form, nor does he train in the cessation of form.
In this way, there is no training in the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor is there training in the cessation of consciousness.
One does not train for the sake of disciplining form, nor for the sake of non-discipline;
likewise, one does not train for the sake of disciplining feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor for the sake of non-discipline.
One does not train for the sake of the transmigration of form, nor for its non-entry.
He does not train for the sake of stability, nor for the sake of non-stability; likewise,
he does not train for the sake of the transition of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor for their entry, nor for their stability, nor for their non-stability.
Training in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not train in the permanence of form, nor does he train in the pleasure of form,
nor does he train in the suffering of form, nor in the beauty of form.
He does not train in the selflessness of form;
nor does he train in the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not train in the pleasantness of consciousness,
nor in the painfulness of consciousness;
one does not train in the purity of consciousness, nor in the selfhood of consciousness.

Training in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not course in an object that is past with respect to form, does not course in an object that is future with respect to form, and does not course in an object that is present with respect to form.
There is no feeling, no perception, no mental formations;
nor does it course in an object that transcends consciousness.
He does not course in a future object of focus, nor does he course in a present object of focus.

Coursing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva contemplates the past through the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of peace, and the aspect of selflessness— thinking, "That which is past is empty."
Thus, [he perceives it as] "peaceful" and "selfless.
Even so, he does not engage [with it].
He examines the future through the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of peace, and the aspect of selflessness—[thinking], "That which is past is empty, peaceful, and selfless."
Even so, he does not course [in that].
He contemplates the present with the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of peace, and the aspect of non-self—[reflecting]: "That which is present is empty, peaceful, and non-self.
Even so, he does not course [in that].

The past is empty, quiescent, and [characterized] by non-self, or by that which belongs not to a self, or by impermanence, or by instability, or by lack of permanence, or by having the nature of transformation;
even so, one does not course therein.
The future is empty, peaceful, and [characterized by] non-self, or non-belonging-to-self, or impermanence, or instability, or lack of permanence, or the nature of change;
even thus one does not course.

The present is empty, peaceful, and [characterized by] non-self, or non-belonging-to-self, or impermanence, or instability, or lack of permanence, or the nature of change—[even thus one does not course].
Even so, he does not course.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for a bodhisattva who courses in this way, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reaches fulfillment.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for a bodhisattva who courses in this way, Māra, the Evil One, finds no opportunity.
Practicing in this way, one recognizes all the works of Māra and is not carried away by those works of Māra.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva practicing in this way does not take form as an object,
nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations; he does not take consciousness as an object.
It does not take name-and-form as its object,
it does not take the range of distorted views as its object,
and it does not take attachment to a self as its object.
It does not take as its object the adherence to a sentient being, nor does it take as its object annihilationism or eternalism,
nor does it take as its object the finite or the infinite.
It does not take as its object form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
it does not take as its object the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
nor does it take dependent origination as its object.
It does not take as its object the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, or space;
it does not take as its object what is true or what is false;
it does not take as its object conjunction or disjunction.
He does not take as an object attachment, aversion, or delusion;
he does not take as an object the abandonment of attachment, aversion, or delusion;
he does not take as an object generosity or stinginess, or ethical discipline or immorality.
It does not take patience and malice as its object; it does not take vigor and laziness as its object;
it does not take meditative concentration and distraction as its object.

It does not take as its object wisdom or lack of wisdom; it does not take as its object the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, or the absence of perversions; nor does it take as its object the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the meditative concentrations and attainments.
It does not take as its object loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity;
it does not take as its object the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of exhaustion, or the knowledge of conditioned formation;
nor does it take as its object the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
He does not take as an object the dharmas of ordinary persons, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas;
he does not take as an object suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path;
nor does he take as an object the superknowledges, knowledge, or vision.
He does not take liberation as an object;
he does not take the knowledge and vision of liberation as an object;
he does not take nirvāṇa as an object.
It does not take as its object the knowledge and vision of the past, future, or present;
it does not take as its object unimpeded knowledge;
it does not take as its object the knowledge of a Buddha.
He does not take as an object the powers and fearlessnesses of a Buddha;
he does not take as an object the purification of the Buddha-field;
he does not take as an object the purity of the marks [of a great man].
He does not take the perfection of the śrāvaka as an object; he does not take the perfection of the pratyekabuddha as an object;
he does not take the perfection of the bodhisattva as an object.
For what reason?

Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all phenomena are without objective support (*nirālambana*). Indeed, among all phenomena, there exists no grasping whatsoever wherein their objective support might reside.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, as long as there is an objective support (ālambana), so long is there attachment (adhyavasāna), so long is there dogmatic adherence (abhiniveśa).
To the extent that there is grasping, to that extent there is appropriation; to the extent that there is appropriation, to that extent there is an objective support.
To that extent do suffering, dejection, intense grief, the sting of sorrow, despair, and lamentation arise;
for as long as there is an objective support (*ālambana*), O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, to that extent there is bondage.
As long as there is an objective referent, so long does the path not exist; as long as there is an objective referent, so long do suffering and mental distress persist.
As long as there is an objective referent, so long do conceptualization, agitation, and proliferation continue.
As long as there is an objective support, so long are there legal disputes, quarrels, and contentions;
as long as there is an objective support, so long is there the darkness of ignorance and delusion;
as long as there is an objective support, so long are there fears. (Vaidya 56)

To the extent that there is an objective support (ālambana), to that same extent there are terrifying things; to the extent that there is an objective support, to that same extent there is the destruction of the snares of Māra and of Māra himself;
to the extent that there is an objective support, to that same extent there is the oppression of suffering and the pursuit of pleasure.
In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, seeing these disadvantages, the bodhisattva does not take any dharma as an object of focus (*ālambana*).
Not taking anything as an object, he does not grasp at any dharma.

He stands neither for the sake of grasping nor for the sake of non-grasping regarding all dharmas; yet, he does not even conceive of that state of being without an object and devoid of mastery as a substantial reality.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not adhere to any dharma, nor does he welcome any dharma; he does not remain intent upon any dharma.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the bodhisattva’s dissociation from all objective supports for dharmas while practicing the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, as a bodhisattva practices, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reaches fulfillment;
neither Māra the Evil One nor the deities belonging to Māra’s host are able to create an obstacle for him.
They do not belong to the retinue of Māra,
nor are they empowered by Māra;
and they find no opportunity to gain entry where they might cause him harm.
Wherever they might seize him and seek to overpower him,
they always recognize all the deeds of Māra,
and he does not fall under the power of those deeds of Māra.
He causes all the abodes of Māra to grow dark;
he stands ready for the subjugation of all non-Buddhist teachers, and he overcomes all other non-Buddhist teachers, including the Carakas and Parivrājakas.
And he becomes unassailable by all opponents.

Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not abide in the conceptualization of form, nor in the discursive differentiation of form. Likewise, he does not abide in the conceptualization of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor in their discursive differentiation.
Furthermore, he neither conceptualizes form nor differentiates it.
In this way, one does not conceptualize or discriminate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one does not conceptualize or discriminate the hindrances or the various views;
one does not conceptualize or discriminate annihilationism or eternalism.
He does not conceptualize or discriminate the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; he does not conceptualize or discriminate passion, hatred, or delusion;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate truth.
He does not falsely conceptualize, nor does he discriminate; he does not conceptualize or discriminate the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, or space;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate conjunction.
He does not conceptualize nor discriminate disjunction;
he does not conceptualize nor discriminate dependent origination;
he does not conceptualize nor discriminate the notion of a self.
He does not conceive of nor discriminate the notion of a sentient being;
he does not conceive of nor discriminate the notion of a living soul;
he does not conceive of nor discriminate the notion of a person.
One does not conceptualize or discriminate between generosity and stinginess, nor between ethical discipline and immorality;
one does not conceptualize or discriminate between patience and malice;
one does not conceptualize or discriminate between diligence and laziness.
He does not conceptualize or discriminate between meditative absorption and distraction;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate between wisdom and lack of wisdom;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate between the absence of perversion, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and the foundations of mindfulness.
He does not conceptualize or discriminate regarding the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, or attainments;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate regarding loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity.

He does not conceptualize or discriminate the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of destruction, or the knowledge of non-conditioning; he does not conceptualize or discriminate the dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, or the dharmas of buddhas;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, or the stage of buddhas.
He does not conceptualize or discriminate the hindrances;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate the knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate unattached knowledge.
He does not conceptualize or discriminate knowledge and liberation;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate liberation or the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate the Buddha-knowledge and the grounds of self-confidence.
He does not conceptualize or discriminate regarding the purity of the marks;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate regarding the purity of the buddha-field;
he does not conceptualize or discriminate regarding the excellence of the śrāvakas.
He does not conceptualize or discriminate the perfection of a pratyekabuddha; he does not conceptualize or discriminate the perfection of a bodhisattva. For what reason?
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when conceptualization exists, there is discursive differentiation;
but where, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, conceptualization does not exist, there is no discursive differentiation.
For all foolish ordinary people, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, arise from conceptual construction; their perceptions arise from discursive differentiation. They construct and they differentiate.
“Conceptualization,” Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is one extreme; “discrimination” is the second extreme.
That wherein there is neither conceptualization nor discrimination—[that is the middle way].
In that regard, there is neither end nor middle.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for one who conceptualizes "middle," that very [conceptualization] becomes an end. As long as there is conceptualization, [there is no middle].
To that extent there is conceptualization;
herein there is no severance of conceptualization.
But where, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization, [there is liberation].
In that regard, there is the "annihilation of the eon.
As for this "annihilation of the eon," O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no annihilation of anything whatsoever here.
For what reason?
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, conceptualization and discrimination are internal, having arisen from discrimination;
their complete subsiding is non-perversion.
That which is non-perversion,
in that there is no cutting whatsoever.
"Complete cutting off," O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a designation for the complete cutting off of suffering.
Furthermore, there would be no cessation of suffering;
there could be a cessation of suffering only if there were some degree of substantial reality to suffering.
This vision of non-attainment is the complete cutting off of suffering;
this thorough knowledge of suffering is what is called the complete cutting off of suffering.
He who neither conceptualizes nor discriminates suffering—
this is the subsiding of suffering; this is the non-arising and non-manifestation of suffering.
Seeing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the bodhisattva does not conceptualize or discriminate any dharma whatsoever.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the thorough understanding of all conceptualization and discrimination for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
