Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for a bodhisattva practicing in this way, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reaches fulfillment;
neither does Māra the Evil One stand as an obstacle to him, nor does the assembly of Māra.
He recognizes each and every māra-activity as it arises,
and he does not fall under the power of those māra-activities as they arise;
he brings about the defeat of Māra, the Evil One, and renders him powerless.
In this way, he makes his faction small and becomes free from fear and terror;
he cannot be assailed by Māras,
and all his paths leading to the miserable states of existence become tranquilized.
The wrong paths are closed off;
he has crossed over all floods and is free from the darkness of delusion.
He becomes one who has attained the eye and serves as light for all sentient beings; he stands for the non-interruption of the lineage of the Buddhas;
and he has attained the path within the equality of paths.
And he becomes one who has compassion for all sentient beings.
His eye regarding phenomena becomes pure;
he is endowed with vigor and free from indolence;
and having attained the power of patience, his mind is free from malice.
He becomes a meditator who meditates without dependence; he possesses attained wisdom, being endowed with penetrative wisdom;
and he is free from remorse, having removed all hindrances.
He becomes dissociated from all the snares of Māra;
he becomes one whose bonds are severed through separation from the entire web of craving;
and he possesses established mindfulness by virtue of the nature of non-forgetfulness.
He possesses pure ethical discipline, having attained the perfection of the purity of ethical discipline; he is established in supreme qualities for the sake of destroying all faults;
and he has attained the empowerment of the power of wisdom through its unshakability.
He becomes unassailable by all Māras and adversaries; he becomes one whose qualities are not lost through the attainment of the purity of all dharmas;
and he becomes confident in the teaching of all dharmas.
He is free from hesitation when approaching an assembly;
he is unattached and practices generous relinquishment through the gift of Dharma;
and his path is thoroughly purified by means of the equality of all paths.
He has cultivated cultivation through the thorough understanding of the wrong path; he is perfumed by perfuming through the nature of pure reality;
and he has purified purification through pure wisdom.
He possesses profound wisdom through his resemblance to the ocean; he is difficult to fathom through his lack of paralysis;
and he is immeasurable through the immeasurability of the ocean of Dharma.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva becomes endowed with these and other qualities, the limits of which cannot be reached.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom does not become deficient in his faculties;
he does not become deficient in form,
nor does he become deficient in enjoyments.
He does not lack a retinue;
he does not lack [a suitable] birth;
he does not lack a [noble] family.
He is not deficient in his location, nor is he reborn in border regions, nor does he fall into the unfavorable conditions.
He does not associate with beings who are impure and whose activities are impure;
he does not let his own mind decline, nor does he fall away from wisdom.
Whatever teachings he hears from others,
he harmonizes them all with the equality of all phenomena (sarvadharma-samatā),
and he remains established for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas and the lineage of omniscience are never interrupted.
He has attained the light regarding the qualities of a Buddha and has become very close to omniscience.
If Māra, the Evil One, should approach him for the purpose of causing him harm, [he will not be shaken].
He reduces that assembly of Māra to ashes, rendering their eloquence severed;
he cuts through all the snares of Māra and becomes invincible to all the hosts and tens of millions of Māras.
Then the Māras, terrified and trembling, flee;
and this thought occurs to Māra, the Evil One: "This one has transcended my domain; he no longer moves within my domain."
"He shall no longer remain within my domain; he shall no longer invade my domain;
and he shall liberate other beings from my domain."
"He will cause [beings] to cross over.
Thereupon, Māra the Evil One grieves, wails, and laments: "This bodhisattva will make me have few partisans. And he enters into a state of weakness.
He becomes distressed, dejected, and full of regret.
And at whatever time, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, [he experiences this].
When one applies oneself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, at that time all the abodes of Māra become dimmed and their splendor diminished;
and the wicked Māras become distressed and dejected, pierced by the thorn of sorrow, struck by the great thorn of profound grief, thinking: "Alas, he will lead these beings away from our domain!"
He will ferry these beings across from our domain;
he will liberate these beings from our domain.
"Alas! He will rescue these beings from our domain;
he will cut these beings free from the snares of Māra; he will lift up these beings who are mired in the mud of sensual desire."
He will liberate beings from the nets of views;
he will rescue beings from the path of hindrances;
he will establish beings upon the true path.
"He will deliver beings from the thicket of views"—
seeing this purpose, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those Māras become distressed, dejected, and pierced by the arrow of grief.
It is just as if, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a man were afflicted and overcome by pain because of a great mass of wealth that had been lost.
Just as a man would be possessed of great physical pain and mental distress,
even so Māra the Evil One becomes sorrowful, dejected, remorseful, and pierced by the arrow of grief;
he finds no pleasure in his own seat.
At whatever time a bodhisattva courses in the perfection of wisdom,
cultivates the perfection of wisdom, and applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom;
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those Māras, the Evil Ones, having gathered together in one place, deliberate: "How shall we act?
What indeed shall we do?
Thus pierced by the arrow of grief born of doubt, they become distressed.
Pierced by the thorn of the sorrow of doubt, they approach the Bodhisattva— who is practicing the perfection of wisdom— in search of a point of attack; yet there,
not even a single hair of the Bodhisattva’s body quivers, much less will there be any alteration in his body or any alteration in his mind.
Mara the Evil One realizes, "My fear and my horripilation have vanished. Having realized this, he exerts his power;
yet, once empowered by that [realization], Mara the Evil One becomes weak, dejected in mind, and overcome by fear.
And he is unable to find an opportunity to gain entry [into him].
It occurs to him: "I myself am not able to find an opportunity to gain entry into him; how much less so my assembly?"
How much more so when others will empower them?
Consequently, those Māras— terrified and deprived of their resolve— will go to their own abodes and remain there brooding, overcome by suffering and dejection.

Furthermore, they are not able to cause even a moment’s delusion of the mind of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for even the duration of a finger-snap, let alone create an obstacle for him.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is [the case] for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Such is the empowerment of the power of wisdom, and he becomes endowed with such an empowerment of the power of wisdom.
Suppose there were all the sentient beings in the entire trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm world-system...
Even if all those Māras were to approach that Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom together with great assemblies of Māra’s retinues, intending to cause him harm,
even all those wicked Māras, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, would not have the power to create an obstacle.
For what reason?
Because at that time, the Bodhisattva is endowed with such an empowerment of the power of wisdom, with the sword of wisdom, and with the weapon of wisdom.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, at that time the Bodhisattva is endowed with inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, and unequaled wisdom.
Therefore, Māra the Evil One is not able to overcome him.
For this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a great weapon, namely the weapon of wisdom;
for this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a great sword, namely the sword of wisdom.
Where there is no access and no domain for the evil Māras, where it is not the ground of the evil Māras—
even those external seers, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, who have attained the four dhyānas;

Or those who, having transcended the realm of Māra— the desire realm— by means of the four formless attainments, are reborn in the Brahma-world and in the four formless states among the classes of beings including the gods.
Even for them, this is beyond comprehension and outside their scope— namely, such wisdom as that which is the ordinary wisdom of a bodhisattva,
let alone the wisdom of one who courses in the perfection of wisdom.
What need is there to mention the Māras, the evil ones, whose domain does not extend to the realm of form or the formless realm?
At that time, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the Bodhisattva has attained the empowerment of strength; he is endowed with great empowerment, namely, by the power of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whoever is endowed with the power of the perfection of wisdom possesses the sharp weapon of wisdom.
They become unassailable by Māras and invincible by evil ones. O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whoever is endowed with the power of wisdom and possesses the sharp weapon of wisdom,
they do not establish a basis anywhere.
They become non-reliant.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when there is reliance, there is movement.
When there is movement, vibration occurs; when there is vibration, conceptual proliferation occurs.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for whomever there is a basis, there is movement, there is vibration, and there is conceptual proliferation.
They fall under the power of Māra the Evil One and remain unliberated from the realm of Māra.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all those beings up to those born at the very peak of existence who are dependent, bound by dependence, and settled in dependence [are likewise].
They too will return again to the realm of Māra;
they are not released from the snares of Māra,
for they are ensnared by the snares of Māra.
For example, Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma,

as well as any others who have taken recourse in the formless realms— being bound by that recourse and dependent upon it— the Bodhisattva, however, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, cultivating the perfection of wisdom, and applying himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, does not take recourse in anything at all.
He becomes non-reliant in all respects.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, at whatever time a bodhisattva dwells engaged in the practice of the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom,
at that time he does not rely upon form.
He does not rely on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not rely on perversions, hindrances, or views; he does not rely on name-and-form.
He does not rely upon the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
he does not rely upon the notions of a self or a sentient being;
he does not rely upon a living soul, a person, or the elements and sense-bases.

He does not rely on earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; he does not rely on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he does not rely on craving, nor does he rely on the craving for existence.
He does not rely on the craving for non-annihilation,
he does not rely on the views of finitude or infinity,
and he does not rely on dependent origination.
He does not rely on generosity or stinginess;
he does not rely on ethical discipline or immorality; he does not rely on patience or malice.
He does not rely on vigor or laziness; he does not rely on meditative concentration or distraction; he does not rely on wisdom or lack of wisdom.
He does not rely on the non-perversions, the right efforts, the immeasurables, or the foundations of mindfulness;
he does not rely on the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the concentrations, or the meditative attainments;
nor does he rely on suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.
He does not rely on the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of destruction, or the knowledge of non-conditioning;
he does not rely on clear knowledge and liberation; nor does he rely on the vision and knowledge of liberation.
He does not rely on the stages of ordinary persons, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas;
he does not rely on the dharmas of ordinary persons, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or perfectly awakened buddhas;
he does not rely on the hindrances.
He does not rely on the non-attachment to the past, future, or present; he does not rely on the equality of the three times;
nor does he rely on the Buddha’s knowledge, powers, and fearlessnesses.
He does not rely on the knowledge of an omniscient one, he does not rely on the perfection of the marks [of a Buddha],
and he does not rely on the perfection of the buddha-field.
He does not rely on the perfection of the array of the śrāvakas, nor does he rely on the perfection of the array of the bodhisattvas;
being non-reliant upon all phenomena, he neither moves nor wavers.
By him, all dependencies are thoroughly eliminated;
being independent, he does not even adhere to the path,
nor does he conceive of non-dependency.
He does not apprehend "this is a reliance," he does not apprehend "here is a reliance," and he does not apprehend or conceive "this belongs to a reliance."
He does not perceive or conceive of "relying on this";

not conceiving of any reliance, not perceiving it, and not adhering to it, he does not resort to any reliance whatsoever, nor does he teach it, nor does he delight in it, nor does he remain fixed upon it with attachment.
Unstained by all forms of reliance and unattached, he attains the purification of reliance regarding all phenomena.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the vision of knowledge regarding the purity of non-reliance on any phenomena for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, by means of which the wicked Māras find no opportunity to enter him,
and he becomes unassailable by all the wicked Māras.
And he overcomes the Evil Māras.
The sixth chapter, "Practice," in the Noble Perfection of Wisdom.

The Seventh Chapter: On the Benefits.

Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, from the very beginning, when a bodhisattva has generated the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he becomes one who has accumulated a vast store of roots of merit,
one who has attended upon many buddhas, and one who has questioned many buddhas.
He has performed his duties toward the Blessed Buddhas,
he is endowed with resolute intention,
and he delights in the sharing of gifts.
He becomes one who values the purity of ethical discipline, he becomes endowed with patience and gentleness,
and he becomes possessed of vigor.
He values the purification of vigor, he values the purification of meditative concentration,
and he possesses wisdom.
One who values the purity of wisdom,

having generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, applies himself to the perfection of wisdom and overcomes the wicked Māras by that power of wisdom, so that those wicked Māras may find no opportunity to gain entry.
And may they not cause me harm;
through his empowerment, the Māras shall find no opportunity for entry, nor shall they stand as obstacles to him.
Nor do they give rise to the thought: "Why should we seek an opportunity against this bodhisattva, or cause him harm?
Even if such a thought should arise in them as an obstacle, [it does not take root].
Then they perceive their own great calamity,
a great fear arises and confronts them, and they become agitated, thinking: "May we not cease to exist altogether."
They withdraw that mind of malice once again;
furthermore, those thoughts of theirs vanish.
By this method as well, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the Māras, the Evil Ones, though they have approached to create obstacles for the Bodhisattva, do not find an opportunity.

Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when the perfection of wisdom is being spoken and taught, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates zeal, resolute intention, reverence, esteem, and the perception of the teacher. Moreover,
when discourse associated with the six perfections is being spoken, no doubt, perplexity, or uncertainty is generated.
Nor, having heard the profound teachings, has he ever given rise to hesitation, sluggishness, or doubt;
nor has he ever accumulated karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma, nor has he ever produced a mind conducive to the ruin of the Dharma.
Furthermore, many other beings are encouraged toward the perfection of wisdom;
they are gladdened and inspired in all six perfections.
Because of the purity of his former mental disposition and because of the non-affliction of his former disposition, the wicked Māras do not appear to create obstacles for him.
Furthermore, the Māras, the Evil Ones, do not find an opportunity to gain entry over him;
he recognizes all the deeds of Māra as they arise one after another,
and he is not carried away by those deeds of Māra.
And he does not fall under the power of Māra’s deeds.
By this method as well, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the wicked Māras do not appear to cause the Bodhisattva any affliction.

Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not course in the sign of the conjunction with form, nor does he course in the sign of the disjunction from form; he does not course in the signs of the conjunction with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the sign of dissociation from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; he does not course in the sign of association with the characteristics of form,
nor does he course in the sign of dissociation from the characteristics of form.
He does not course in the sign of the conjunction of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

he does not course in the sign of the disjunction of those characteristics; nor does he course in the sign of the conjunction of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
He does not course in the sign of the purity of form, nor does he course in the sign of the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the sign of the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not course in the sign of the purity of the objective support of form, nor does he course in the sign of the absence of purity of the objective support of form.

He does not course in the sign of the purity of the objective support of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does he course in the sign of the purity of the objective support of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He courses in the conjunction with the purity of the arising of form.
He does not course in the dissociation from the arising and purification of form;
he does not course in the dissociation from the arising and purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does he course in the dissociation from the arising and purification of consciousness.
He does not course in the conjunction with the purity of the intrinsic nature of form as an object,

nor does he course in the disjunction from the purity of the intrinsic nature of form as an object. He does not course in the conjunction with the purity of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as objects, nor [does he course in their disjunction].
He does not course in the dissociation from the purity of the intrinsic nature of the objective support of consciousness;
he does not course in the purity of the intrinsic nature of form, nor in the purity of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the conjunction with the purity of the intrinsic nature of the objective support of form,

nor does he course in the disjunction from the purity of the intrinsic nature of the objective support of form; he does not course in the conjunction with the purity of the intrinsic nature of the objective support of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he course in the disjunction from the purity of the intrinsic nature of the objective support of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the purity of form—past, future, or present; nor does he course in the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—past, future, or present.
He does not course in the purity of the past, future, or present objects of focus (ālambana) of form.
He does not course in the purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness regarding the past, future, or present;
he does not course in the conjunction with the purification of form regarding the past, future, or present,
nor does he course in the conjunction with the purification of form regarding the past, future, or present.
He does not course in the conjunction with the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, whether past, future, or present;
nor does he course in the disjunction from the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, whether past, future, or present.
He does not course in the conjunction with the purity of form as an object, whether past, future, or present.

He does not course in the dissociation from the purity of past, future, or present objects of form; nor in the dissociation from the purity of past, future, or present objects of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Coursing thus, he is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from form.
It is neither conjoined nor disjoined with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with name-and-form;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the states of perversions and views.
It is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with passion, hatred, or delusion;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the notions of self, sentient being, life-force, person, existence, or non-existence.
It is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from annihilation or permanence;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the elements and sense-bases;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
It is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from dependent origination;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the five strands of sensual pleasure;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from affliction or purification.
It is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from generosity and stinginess;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from ethical discipline and immorality;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from patience and malice.
It is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from vigor or laziness;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from meditative concentration or distraction;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from wisdom or the state of a mind characterized by poor wisdom.
It is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the non-perversions, the right efforts, the foundations of mindfulness, or the bases of psychic power;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the concentrations, or the meditative attainments;
it is neither conjoined nor [disjoined] with suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.
One is dissociated [from them].
One is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from calm abiding and insight.
One is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from knowledge and liberation.
It is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the knowledge and vision of liberation;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the superknowledges;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
It is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of exhaustion, or the knowledge of non-formative activity;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
it is neither conjoined nor disjoined with the Buddha-knowledge, powers, and intrepidities.
It is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the perfection of the marks;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the arrays of the Buddha-fields;
it is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
It is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from the perfection of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
For what reason?
Because, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all dharmas do not appear through conjunction, nor through disjunction.
For "conjunction," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is a term for permanence.
"Disjunction" means annihilation.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, among all phenomena there is no realization whatsoever by which they might be joined or disjoined.
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, among all phenomena nothing is present for the sake of conjunction, nor for the sake of disjunction.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if there were anyone among phenomena who could either join them together or separate them, or if one could find a maker or a cause of phenomena, or an arouser or an instigator of them, [then this would be possible].
Or the originator or the one who causes to originate, or the feeler or the one who causes to feel,
or the knower or the one who causes to know.
Whether as a uniter or a disuniter, the Tathāgata might designate: "This one is the maker or the cause of making of these phenomena;
the arouser or the cause of arousing."
Whether it be the originator or the one who causes to originate, the feeler or the one who causes to feel,
the knower or the one who causes to know.
Whether it be one who joins together or one who separates;
since, O Vikrāntavikrāmin, no one is present for the sake of joining or separating any phenomena,
therefore there is no one among phenomena who is an agent or a cause of action.
Whether it be one who raises up or causes to raise up, one who originates or causes to originate, or one who feels or causes to feel.
Whether as a knower or one who causes knowledge,
as one who joins together or one who disjoins, [the Tathāgata] is not apprehended;
yet, while being unapprehended, the Tathāgata designates [himself].
For all phenomena, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, arise from perversion;
yet perversion is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from anything.
Why is that?
For indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, no objective basis for perversion is apprehended,
nor is its arising apprehended.
Why is that?
For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, perversion is unreal, false, deceptive,
and empty; nor is there any dharma to be found therein that could be called "perversion."
"O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, 'perversion' is this misapprehension of sentient beings;
it is this deception of sentient beings; it is this unreal imagination of sentient beings."
This conceiving, this agitation, and this conceptual proliferation belong to sentient beings.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as when a young child is teased with an empty fist and perceives it as real;
in the very same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, foolish ordinary people, deluded and teased by the perversion of nihilism, think, "This is real."
Perceiving the unreal as real, those seized by perversion become difficult to liberate from that perversion.
Thus, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all foolish ordinary people—neither joined nor disjoined [to reality]—wander about bound by fetters;
they imagine this to be "joining."
They perceive them as "conjunction," they see what is established as "conjunction," and they become attached to them as "conjunction."
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, wherever there is conjunction, there is disjunction. Furthermore, he who does not perceive conjunction, does not conceive of it, and does not adhere to it—
He does not even conceive of dissociation;
he is utterly liberated.
If he were to conceive of dissociation, or perceive it, or become attached to it, [he would not be liberated].
He would indeed be bound and not liberated.
In this regard, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, seeing this significance of the matter, a bodhisattva is neither bound by nor liberated from any dharma;
nor does he stand for the sake of being bound to or liberated from any dharma whatsoever.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the thorough knowledge of conjunction and disjunction of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva swiftly attains the further shore of all phenomena.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not course in the non-attachment to form;
he does not course in the non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the purification of the non-attachment to form.
He does not course in the purification of non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the objective support of non-attachment to form; he does not course in the objective support of non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the non-attachment and non-union with form, nor does he course in the non-attachment and non-separation from form.
He does not course in the non-attachment and non-union with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the non-attachment to consciousness nor in its dissociation from it;
he does not course in the purity of the non-attachment to form nor in its association with it, nor does he course in the dissociation from the purity of the non-attachment to form.
He does not course in the conjunction with the purity of non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does he course in the disjunction from the purity of non-attachment to consciousness.
He does not course in the conjunction with the purity of the objective support of form.
He does not course in the dissociation from the purity of the objective support of form;
he does not course in the dissociation from the purity of the objective supports of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does he course in the dissociation from the purity of the objective support of consciousness.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all these signs—whether they be stirred, flickered, practiced, or pursued—have been fully understood by the bodhisattva;
he no longer moves or pursues anything at all.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice in the attachment to form as past, future, or present;
nor does he practice in the non-attachment to form as past, future, or present.
He does not practice in the attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as past, future, or present.
He does not course in attachment to consciousness as past, future, or present;
he does not course in the purification of form as past, future, or present, nor does he course in the impurity of form as past, future, or present.

He does not course in the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness regarding the past, future, or present; nor does he course in the impurity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness regarding the past, future, or present.
He does not course in the purity of the unattached object of form regarding the past, future, or present.
He does not course in the purity of the non-attached object of focus regarding form—past, future, or present;
nor does he course in the purity of the non-attached object of focus regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—past, future, or present;
nor does he course in the purity of the non-attached object of focus regarding consciousness—past, future, or present.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any practice.
This non-practice, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the practice of a bodhisattva regarding all practices.
And this is the entrance into wisdom for one practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva swiftly attains the fulfillment of the qualities of omniscience.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice with the thought that form is uncovered,
nor does he practice with the thought that form is not uncovered.
He does not practice with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness are uncovered, nor does he practice with the thought that consciousness is ununcovered.
One does not practice with the thought that form is peaceful,
nor does one practice with the thought that form is not peaceful; and the same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He does not practice with the thought that consciousness is peaceful, nor does he practice with the thought that consciousness is not peaceful.
He does not practice with the thought that form is by nature uncovered.
He does not practice with the thought that form is not open by nature;
nor does he practice with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness are open by nature.
He does not practice with the thought that consciousness is by nature unopened;
he does not practice with the thought that form is by nature unpeaceful or that it is unpeaceful;
nor does he do so regarding feeling, perception, or mental formations.

He does not course in the notion that consciousness is "quiescent by nature" or "not quiescent. He does not course in the notion that form—past, future, or present—is "separated from its nature" or "quiescent by nature.
Nor does he course in the notion that form—past, future, or present—is "not separated from its nature" or "not quiescent by nature."

There is no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness— whether past, future, or present— that courses in being either naturally secluded or naturally peaceful; nor does consciousness— whether past, future, or present— course in being either naturally secluded or naturally peaceful.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva swiftly attains the fulfillment of the qualities of omniscience.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not conceive of form; likewise,
he does not conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not conceive of the purity of form,
nor does he conceive of the purity of the objective support of form;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One does not conceive of the purity of consciousness,
nor does one conceive of the purity of the objective support of consciousness.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
he does not adhere to form; likewise, he does not adhere to feeling, perception, or mental formations.
One does not adhere to consciousness;
one does not adhere to the purity of form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
The purification of consciousness does not adhere;
it does not adhere to the purification of the objective support of form.
The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He does not become attached to the purification of the object of consciousness.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva quickly attains the fulfillment of the qualities of omniscience.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva draws near to the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
Of the four fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
and great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva draws near to the thirty-two marks of a great person;
he draws near to having skin of a golden color;
he draws near to the infinite radiance of a Tathāgata.
He becomes near to the elephant-like gaze;
he becomes near to the state of having the crown of the head invisible;
he becomes near to the knowledge and vision that is unattached regarding the past, future, and present.
He becomes near to the miracle of the Tathāgata’s exhortation and instruction;
he becomes near to the prophecy of unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past, future, and present.
Moving in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva swiftly attains the complete fulfillment of all the qualities of a Buddha.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva quickly attains the purification of a buddha-field and swiftly acquires the perfection of the array of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva does not abide in form.
He does not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not abide in name-and-form;
he does not abide in perversions, hindrances, or views.
It does not abide in the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm;
it does not abide in the realm of a self, nor does it abide in the realm of sentient beings.
He does not abide in the notion of a person or a living being;
he does not abide in the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness;
nor does he abide in the elements or the sense bases.
He does not abide in affliction or purification;
he does not abide in dependent origination;
he does not abide in renunciation or stinginess.
He does not abide in either ethical discipline or immorality; he does not abide in either patience or malice; he does not abide in either vigor or laziness.
He does not abide in meditative concentration or distraction;
he does not abide in wisdom or ignorance;
he does not abide in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, or the factors of enlightenment.
He does not abide in the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, or attainments;
he does not abide in suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path;
he does not abide in the knowledge of exhaustion, non-arising, or conditioned phenomena.
He does not abide in calm abiding and insight; he does not abide in the superknowledges;
he does not abide in knowledge and liberation.
He does not abide in the stages of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the samyaksaṃbuddha;
he does not abide in the dharmas of ordinary persons, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas;
nor does he abide in nirvāṇa.
He does not abide in the Buddha’s knowledge, powers, and fearlessnesses;
he does not abide in unimpeded knowledge;
he does not abide in the vision of knowledge regarding the past, future, and present.
He does not abide in the excellence of the Buddha-field; he does not abide in the excellence of the array of Śrāvakas;
he does not abide in the excellence of the array of Bodhisattvas.
For what reason?
Because, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all phenomena are non-abiding. Indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, no abiding place for any phenomena exists.
For what reason?
Because, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all dharmas are indeed without abode;
because they are without abode, they do not stand.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if there were a foundation for phenomena, or if there were a storehouse or an immutable essence of phenomena, the Tathāgata would have demonstrated that foundation of phenomena, saying: "This is the foundation of phenomena."
"This is the storehouse of phenomena; this is the accumulation of phenomena.
However, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, because all phenomena are non-abiding, without a storehouse, and without accumulation, [they are such].
Therefore, no dharma whatsoever is immutable.
For that reason, the Tathāgata does not designate any dharma as a foundation, a storehouse, or an accumulation.
Indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, dharmas are not fully established.
Nor is there any intrinsic nature whatsoever;
because phenomena are impossible and lack ultimate establishment, nothing at all remains.
Therefore it is said: "All phenomena are non-abiding."
By way of non-abiding and by way of non-locus, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, all phenomena are unestablished. There is no abiding, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for any phenomena.
It is just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for the four great rivers flowing from Lake Anavatapta, there is no locus other than the great ocean.
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, there is no abiding of all phenomena,

as long as they do not exhaust themselves through non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*). "Non-conditioning," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, means that therein there is neither a place, nor a non-place, nor a basis.
In all cases, this enumeration does not exist.
Whether it be called a "place," or a "foundation," or a "non-place," or a "volitional formation"—Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is taught as an enumeration.
This is merely a demonstration of the activity of sentient beings; it is designated as a non-place, a place, or a foundation.
In the absence of volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*), this calculation no longer applies;
therefore it is said that "all phenomena are non-abiding.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the bodhisattva’s yoga of the non-abiding of all phenomena.
For one who courses in the perfection of wisdom;
thus coursing, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva quickly fulfills all the qualities of omniscience and draws near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He quickly approaches the seat of awakening,
quickly attains the knowledge of omniscience,
and quickly achieves the perfection of knowledge regarding the past, future, and present.
And he swiftly reaches the further shore of all the movements, activities, and fluctuations of the minds of all sentient beings.
Therefore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish the welfare [of others],
who wishes to give gifts to all sentient beings,
and who wishes to satisfy all sentient beings with the gift of Dharma—
Desiring to shatter the shell of ignorance for all sentient beings, desiring to bestow upon all sentient beings the great wisdom that is the wisdom of a Buddha,
and desiring to be compassionate toward all sentient beings.
by one who wishes to be a seeker of the welfare of all sentient beings,
who wishes to bring about an abundance of Dharma for all sentient beings, and who wishes to bring about an abundance of material enjoyments for all sentient beings;

Desiring to bring about an abundance of ethical discipline for all sentient beings, desiring to bring about an abundance of patience and gentleness for all sentient beings, and desiring to bring about an abundance of vigor for all sentient beings;
Desiring to provide for all sentient beings an abundance of meditative concentration, desiring to provide for all sentient beings an abundance of wisdom,
and desiring to provide for all sentient beings an abundance of liberation;
By one who desires to bring about the abundance of rebirth in heaven for all sentient beings; by one who desires to bring about the abundance of knowledge and liberation for all sentient beings;
by one who desires to bring about the abundance of the vision of the knowledge of liberation for all sentient beings.
One who desires to bring about an abundance free from hindrances for all sentient beings; one who desires to bring about an abundance of the Buddha-dharma for all sentient beings;
and one who desires to bring about an abundance of the perfection of all virtuous qualities for all sentient beings.

One who desires to turn the wheel of Dharma— which has never before been turned by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world— and who desires to engage in discourse on the Dharma and to receive a prophecy regarding the stage of Buddhahood;
One who wishes to provide a prediction regarding the stage of a śrāvaka, one who wishes to provide a prediction regarding the stage of a pratyekabuddha,

and one who wishes to stimulate the roots of merit from the former vows of all sentient beings, should train in this perfection of wisdom, strive, exert effort, and apply themselves to the yoga of cultivating the perfection of wisdom.
It must be so.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, I do not perceive any other dharma among all dharmas that brings about such rapid fulfillment for a bodhisattva as this application and practice directed toward the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught here.
The non-abandonment of the dwelling, namely, for the sake of the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, regarding those bodhisattvas who practice this perfection of wisdom, it should be understood that they have reached the culmination: "These bodhisattvas are close to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for whomever this perfection of wisdom shall even come within the range of hearing, [they too are near].
Having heard it, they will have faith, they will rejoice, and they will produce the perception of reality;

I declare that their roots of goodness also bring about unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— one must reach the conclusion that these sons of good family have indeed accumulated a great store of wisdom.
or daughters of good family,
will grasp other roots of merit as well.
And, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those bodhisattvas into whose hands this exposition of the chapter on the skill in means of the perfection of wisdom shall come—
Furthermore, although some among them may not have received a prediction in the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
nevertheless it should be understood that they are close to receiving a prediction; before long, they will obtain a prediction in the very presence [of the Buddhas].

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if there were beings who, having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action, abide in them; in that case, this conclusion should be reached: these beings are indeed close to rebirth in Uttarakuru.
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if this perfection of wisdom should become an object of laughter for any bodhisattva whatsoever,
it should be known that he is near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if there were beings who bestow gifts and become those who have relinquished all attachment,
who gather in beings through generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency of purpose,
and who maintain ethical discipline.
And they become free from pride; one should reach the conclusion that these beings will quickly become possessed of great wealth and born into high families.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if there were beings who practice generosity and maintain ethical discipline, who are perfected in morality, perfected in patience, established in vigor and meditative concentration, and endowed with wisdom.
They generate loving-kindness toward sentient beings,
they encourage sentient beings to undertake ethical discipline,
and they accumulate karma that leads to sovereignty.
It should be understood that these will soon exercise the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

In the very same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it should be understood that whichever bodhisattva comes to possess this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in his hand, he will swiftly approach the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as when, on the fifteenth day of the full moon, the wheel-treasure appears before a Kṣatriya king who is seated in his court for the administration of justice;
in that case, it should be known: "He will become a universal monarch, and soon his seven treasures will appear."

In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it should be known that for whichever bodhisattva this chapter on the perfection of wisdom comes into their hands, they will quickly come to be endowed with the objective supports of omniscience.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if there were beings who would be endowed with superior roots of goodness, who would possess excellent conduct, and who would have noble aspirations, yet in whom a perception of revulsion toward this human existence remains established.
They are endowed with ethical discipline,
they perform services for the great multitude,
and they aspire for rebirth among the gods.
It should be understood that these will quickly be reborn to dwell together with the gods of the Four Great Kings,
and there they will exercise sovereignty.

O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those who are endowed with exceptionally pure roots of merit and possess superior roots of merit, who first give gifts and afterwards eat themselves— [it should be known that they will attain this].
Furthermore, they perform the tasks of other sentient beings first and their own afterwards;
they are neither stained by unrighteous passion nor stained by uneven passion.
If they desire sovereignty and lordship over the gods,
it should be known that before long they will exercise unshakable sovereignty and lordship over the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
and they will become Śakras, the Indras of the gods.

In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when this perfection of wisdom comes to any bodhisattva whatsoever, it should be understood as certain that he will swiftly attain mastery, sovereignty, and power over all dharmas.
Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it should be known that those beings who have attained the four divine abodes will quickly be reborn in the Brahma-world;
even so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it should be understood of one [who possesses this samādhi].
If this teaching on the perfection of wisdom should come to any bodhisattva,
it should be known that he will swiftly set in motion the wheel of Dharma.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as when the months of the rainy season have arrived, this great earth becomes moist in dependence upon the clouds;
and as it rains in succession,
being drenched by the rain, they pour down water again and again from above.
By which many follow with enthusiasm,
and which saturate the surface of this great earth;
thus this great earth becomes both internally moistened and supple.
And just as water, when poured from above, saturates both the lowlands and the highlands,
so too this great earth, being drenched from above by clouds, saturates the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and forest trees.
Being thus moistened, they shed many branches, leaves, and foliage, and become abundant with flowers and fruits;
at that time, this great earth emits a delightful fragrance.
In this way, at that time, this great earth becomes adorned with flowers, fruits, springs, and ponds.
Consequently, both humans and non-humans become delighted as they enjoy those flowers and fruits and smell that fragrance.
In the very same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when this perfection of wisdom becomes manifest to a bodhisattva and he applies himself to yoga in this perfection of wisdom, [the same occurs].
It should be known, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that before long this bodhisattva will be saturated with the knowledge of omniscience;
he will open up the knowledge of omniscience and he will illuminate the knowledge of omniscience.
And by that, he will moisten sentient beings for the sake of illuminating the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as, for example, those beings who have been born in the abode of the nāga king Anavatapta release the four great rivers which satisfy the great ocean;
even so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for those bodhisattvas into whose hands this perfection of wisdom shall come, [the same occurs].
Those who do not train in this [perfection] will all rain down great streams of Dharma,
by which they will satisfy all sentient beings with the gift of Dharma.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if any beings who approach Sumeru, the king of mountains, all become of one color— that is to say, they become golden-colored.
In the very same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those bodhisattvas into whose hands this exposition of the perfection of wisdom shall fall [will likewise become of one color].
They shall all go to a single destination, namely, the destination of the Tathāgata, the destination of omniscience.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as, for example, the great ocean Sāgara is the sustainer of all waters,

and all water constantly flows into it; even so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whichever bodhisattva this exposition of the perfection of wisdom comes into the hands of, [he shall likewise receive all dharmas].

One should reach the conclusion that he will swiftly attain the ocean-like nature of all phenomena, the receptacle-nature of all phenomena, and the convergence of all phenomena; and swiftly, through the conventional designation of "Dharma," he will become unshakable.

Just as, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the orb of the sun, when it rises, illuminates all directions with its radiance, even so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva practicing this perfection of wisdom stands present for the purpose of providing illumination of the Dharma for all sentient beings;
thus rising up here, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the bodhisattva.
He stands present through the illumination of the roots of virtue of all sentient beings;
he becomes worthy of offerings for all sentient beings;
and he attains the purification of the field of merit for all sentient beings.
He becomes approachable by all sentient beings,
and he becomes worthy of worship and praise by all sentient beings.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva training in this perfection of wisdom trains in preeminence,
and he trains for the sake of purifying the path to nirvāṇa for all sentient beings.
For what reason?
For this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the foremost training, the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the unsurpassed, the peerless— namely, this training in the perfection of wisdom.
Training in this, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva attains the perfection of all trainings and,
having undertaken all trainings, rises above them.
He becomes a teacher of all trainings and a bearer of all trainings;
for in this training, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, have trained, will train, and are training.

And it is upon this training that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, being well-established, have fully proclaimed and continue to fully proclaim the unsurpassed purity of training for all sentient beings.
For what reason is that?
For this training, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is one that transcends the entire world—namely, the training in the perfection of wisdom.
It is a training superior to all the world, a training in self-becoming for the entire world—namely, the training in the perfection of wisdom.
When training in the perfection of wisdom, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva does not train in any phenomenon whatsoever, whether mundane or supramundane.
Whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether with outflows or without outflows, whether blameworthy or blameless.
He does not produce attachment anywhere;
he dwells in non-attachment toward all phenomena.
For what reason?
For all dharmas, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, are unattached, unbound, and unliberated;
they do not appear through attachment to any dharma, nor through bondage.
For form, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
Name-and-form is unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The perversions, views, and hindrances are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
Attachment, aversion, and delusion are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The six internal sense bases are unattached, unbound, and unliberated. The six external sense bases are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The realms of desire, form, and formlessness are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The realm of self and the realm of sentient beings are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
Dependent origination is unattached, unbound, and unliberated.

Defilement and purification are unattached, unbound, and unliberated. Likewise, renunciation and avarice, morality and immorality, patience and malice, vigor and indolence, meditative concentration and distraction, wisdom and false wisdom are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the immeasurables, and the non-perversions are unliberated.
The faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, concentrations, and meditative attainments are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The knowledges of non-arising, exhaustion, and conditioned formation are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The liberation from ignorance is unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The engagement with the superknowledges is unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
Knowledge, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The dharmas of ordinary persons, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
Nirvāṇa is unattached, unbound, and unliberated.
The Buddha’s wisdoms, powers, and fearlessnesses are unattached, unbound, and unfreed;
the unhindered knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present are unattached, unbound, and unfreed.
For what reason?
For indeed, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, no bondage of all dharmas is apprehended;
for all dharmas, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, are unattached and unbound.
Therefore, liberation is not apprehended for them.
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, because they are unattached, there is no one to liberate them;
rather, it is precisely this vision of all dharmas [that constitutes liberation].
This is called the vision of unattached knowledge.
"Unattached," Suvikrāntavikrāmin, means the non-apprehension of attachment.
It is unattached by virtue of its lack of attachment.
It is called "unattached" because of its state of non-attachment;
herein nothing is found that could either be joined or bound.
And because that which is joined or bound is not apprehended,
for that reason it is called "unattached.
It is "unbound," O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, because of the non-apprehension of bondage.
Because there is no reality to bondage, it is said to be unbound;
for therein no bondage exists,
nor is anyone found therein who is bound.
And because that which is bound is not apprehended, for that reason it is said to be unbound;
and that which is unattached is unbound.
Whence can there be liberation for him who neither clings nor is bound? He is liberated, detached, cooled, and utterly freed.
In that state, there is no further bondage;
therefore, it is called "liberated.
For him, no further liberation exists.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is the entry into the knowledge and vision of all phenomena— unattached, unbound, and liberated— for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, a bodhisattva draws near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening,
and he swiftly attains the knowledge of omniscience.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, I establish this seal for the sake of cutting through the doubts of those bodhisattvas who are devoted to the perfection of wisdom and who course in the perfection of wisdom.

Suvikrāntavikrāmin, I myself shall empower this exposition of the seal; my disciples are not capable of maintaining this seal of the perfection of wisdom in the future time, in the final age, during the last five hundred years.

Then the Blessed One addressed five hundred bodhisattvas, headed by the noble caravan leader Bhadrapāla and the bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "O sons of good family, are you able, after the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa,
in the future time, in the final period, during the last five hundred years at the time when the true Dharma is disappearing?"

While the destruction of the true Dharma is underway and the time has grown short, who will be able to uphold this treasury of the Dharma-jewels of the Tathāgata— accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons— which is preceded by the perfection of wisdom, originates from the perfection of wisdom, and is established upon the perfection of wisdom— and to proclaim it extensively to others?

When this had been said, the Bodhisattvas spoke thus to the Blessed One: "We are able, O Blessed One, to uphold this unsurpassed treasury of the Dharma-jewel of the Tathāgata— which has been brought forth through many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, which is preceded by the perfection of wisdom, originates from the perfection of wisdom, and is established upon the perfection of wisdom— and to proclaim it in detail to others."
Moreover, Blessed One, although that time will be one of great fear, a vast wilderness, and exceedingly terrible,

for the most part at that time sentient beings will be possessed of karma conducive to the disappearance of the true Dharma; they will be greedy with improper greed, stained by improper passion and stained by passion for what is unrighteous, their minds overwhelmed by envy and greed, and they will be wrathful and fierce.

They were harsh, foul-mouthed, deceitful, fraudulent, and practitioners of illusion; they lived unrighteously, being full of quarreling, reviling, disputing, and strife; they remained without restraint, greedy, overcome by greed, indolent, lacking in vigor, with stolen mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension;

they were garrulous, loquacious, and impudent, with evil deeds concealed within their hearts; they possessed an abundance of passion, hatred, and delusion, and were overwhelmed by the darkness and gloom of the eggshell of ignorance.
They will act in accordance with the faction of Māra and become adversaries;
they will possess minds and conduct that do not rise up toward this profound Dharma-Vinaya, this treasury of the jewel of the Dharma.

Nevertheless, O Blessed One, we are able to uphold this unsurpassed treasury of the jewel of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, which was brought forth through roots of merit accumulated over many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
And those beings who, at that time of the end, though they be very few in number, shall be seekers of these dharmas and desirous of training in these dharmas—
They are honest, upright, and free from deceit;
they would even sacrifice their lives,
but would never become adversaries of these teachings.
Nor would they reject these dharmas, nor would they turn their backs on these dharmas;
we shall accomplish their welfare.
And we shall provide encouragement;
we shall demonstrate these very qualities,
we shall inspire them, and we shall gladden them.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One empowered this empowerment of the Dharma, the exposition of the perfection of wisdom;
and for the sake of cutting the snares of Māra the Evil One regarding this Dharma-discourse, he established his empowerment. Then, the Blessed One manifested a smile.
Just as this trichiliocosm was suffused with a great radiance,
so too did the gods see humans, and humans saw the gods.
The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas who had assembled there all scattered divine flowers over the Blessed One and cast down divine robes.
And they raised a great roar and cry: "Aha! This is indeed a great empowerment bestowed by the Tathāgata, wherein the evil Māras have no access;
for by this empowerment of the Dharma, all the snares of Māra have been severed.
These sons of good family and daughters of good family may expect to be further free from fear of the evil Māras."
Those who shall uphold, recite, and extensively proclaim this Dharma-discourse to others—
those bodhisattvas will have crossed over;
and those who uphold this Dharma-discourse will defeat Māra, the Evil One, together with his army.
And they will proclaim it in detail to others.
Then the Blessed One said this to the bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "It is so, Suvikrāntavikrāmin; it is just so, as these sons of the gods have spoken."
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, when this Dharma discourse is being spoken by the Tathāgata, the boundary of the wicked Māras has been set. Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin,
those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up, retain, recite, and extensively proclaim this Dharma discourse to others— herein indeed [they are protected].
There shall be no access for Māra, the Evil One; and those sons of good family and daughters of good family shall be unassailable by Māras, the Evil Ones.
They shall have struck down the adversaries that are Māras and shall have emerged victorious from the battle.
Those who shall take up this Dharma-discourse, uphold it, recite it,
and reveal it in detail to others—
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this Dharma-discourse will certainly not fall into the hands of beings who are defiled.
Nor is it for those bound by the snares of Māra.
This, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, is the ground of the well-bred;
this is not the ground of the untrained, nor the ground of those who are not well-bred.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is just as if those who will be noble elephants or noble horses do not perform service for petty kings,
nor do they even come into the sight of cruel people.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin, for universal monarchs there appear such noble elephants and noble horses;
they rise up for their enjoyment, for their service, and for their attendance,
for they exist for the enjoyment of the universal monarch kings.
In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, these kinds of Dharma-discourses will come into the hands of those beings who are like well-bred horses among men for their enjoyment.
For example, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, it is like the nāga king Uposadha, the nāga king Supratiṣṭhita, and the nāga king Airāvaṇa.
They do not approach for the enjoyment of humans, nor do they approach to be seen by humans,
nor do they approach for the enjoyment or consumption of other gods.
Those nāga kings approach for the enjoyment of the noble steeds of the gods;

and in whatever manner Śakra, the lord of the gods, approaches having formed a military array, in that very same manner the nāga kings also approach for the sake of enjoyment, having formed a corresponding array.

In the same way, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those who will become lords of men, lords of persons— for them these Dharma-discourses will serve as objects of enjoyment and utility, namely through their recitation, teaching, and thorough proclamation; and for them these Dharma-discourses will be great arrays, great manifestations, and great lights of the Dharma.
And they will experience great joy in the Dharma regarding these dharma-discourses;
they will be endowed with great joy and gladness,
those who uphold even a single method of this dharma-discourse.
How much more so for those who, having caused it to be written out in its entirety and completion, shall uphold it, honor it, and cause it to be widely disseminated—
they are lords among men, they are thoroughbred men.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, they will indeed be taken into the care of this Dharma-discourse.
This is the non-path for those who are not noble;
this too, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, I speak for the sake of cutting through all doubts.

Furthermore, while this Dharma discourse was being spoken by the Blessed One, many immeasurable bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Immeasurable and incalculable beings also gave rise to the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and they were declared by the Tathāgata to be destined for awakening.
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin, along with the fourfold assembly, were uplifted in mind.
And the world, including its gods, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. Thus [it was said].
The seventh chapter of the Noble Prajñāpāramitā, titled "The Chapter on Benefits."
The Noble Sūtra of the Questions of Suvikrāntavikrāmin: An Exposition on the Perfection of Wisdom.
The Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Two Thousand Five Hundred Lines, spoken by the Blessed One, is completed.

That which, through omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), leads the Śrāvakas seeking peace to tranquility; and that which, through the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), accomplishes the welfare of the world for those who act for the benefit of beings.
Homage to the Mother of the Buddha, who is accompanied by the hosts of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, and through whom the Munis declare this entire universe in all its aspects. // 1 //
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. (2)
